title: Scaled Dot-Product Attention, Step by Step
text: This is Part 4, the first of four articles on attention. After tokenization and embeddings, every token is a vector. Attention is the operation that lets those vectors talk to each other, and it is the core of every Transformer. The next articles cover masking, encoder-decoder and cross-attention, multi-head attention, and the cost of attention (KV cache, GQA, MLA).

title: Scaled Dot-Product Attention, Step by Step
text:
The problem attention solves
After the embedding layer, the word “bank” has the same vector in “river bank” and in “bank account”. The vector knows nothing about its neighbours. A language model needs each token’s representation to be updated using the other tokens in the sequence.
Attention does exactly this, with one idea:

Each token builds its new vector as a weighted average of information from all tokens, where the weights are computed from the content itself.

A recurrent network passes information along the sequence one step at a time. Attention instead lets every position look at every other position directly. This is the design the original Transformer paper (Vaswani et al., 2017) proposed: an architecture built on attention alone, with no recurrence and no convolutions.

title: Scaled Dot-Product Attention, Step by Step
text:
Intuition: a soft dictionary lookup
A Python dictionary does a hard lookup: the query must match a key exactly, and you get back one value.
d = {"cat": v_cat, "dog": v_dog}
d["cat"]            # exact match -> exactly one value
Attention is a soft lookup. The query is compared with every key, each comparison gives a similarity score, and what you get back is a blend of all the values, weighted by those scores. Each token plays three roles:








Role
Name
Plain-language meaning




What I am looking for
Query (Q)
“Which other tokens are relevant to me?”


What I advertise for matching
Key (K)
“This is what I look like to a query.”


What I hand over if chosen
Value (V)
“This is the content you get if you attend to me.”



Why three separate roles instead of using the token vector directly? Because “what makes me a good match” and “what I contribute once matched” are different jobs, and the model is free to learn them separately. It also makes attention asymmetric: token A can attend strongly to token B without B attending to A.

title: Scaled Dot-Product Attention, Step by Step
text:
The computation, with shapes
Let a sequence have \(n\) tokens, each represented by a \(d\)-dimensional vector. Stack them into a matrix \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}\) (one row per token). Attention uses three learned projection matrices to produce queries, keys and values:
\[
Q = X W^Q, \qquad K = X W^K, \qquad V = X W^V
\]
with \(W^Q, W^K \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d_k}\) and \(W^V \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d_v}\). Then:
\[
\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) \;=\; \text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{Q K^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) V
\]

Scores. \(QK^\top\) takes the dot product of every query with every key. A large dot product means “these two vectors point in a similar direction”, which is the model’s notion of relevance.
Scale. Divide by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) (explained below).
Softmax, per row. Turn each row of scores into positive weights that sum to 1. Row \(i\) says how much token \(i\) attends to each token.
Weighted sum. Multiply by \(V\): row \(i\) of the output is the weighted average of all value vectors, using row \(i\) of \(A\) as the weights.

title: Scaled Dot-Product Attention, Step by Step
text:
A worked example
Three tokens, \(d_k = d_v = 2\). Suppose the projections produced:
\[
Q = K = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad
V = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}
\]
Scores \(S = QK^\top\) (entry \((i,j)\) = dot product of query \(i\) with key \(j\)):
\[
S = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}
\]
Scale by \(\sqrt{d_k} = \sqrt{2} \approx 1.414\), then softmax each row. For row 1: \(\text{softmax}(0.71,\ 0,\ 0.71) = (0.40,\ 0.20,\ 0.40)\). Doing all rows (rounded to two decimals):
\[
A \approx \begin{pmatrix} 0.40 & 0.20 & 0.40 \\ 0.20 & 0.40 & 0.40 \\ 0.25 & 0.25 & 0.50 \end{pmatrix}
\]
Weighted sum \(O = AV\). Row 1 is \(0.40\,(1,0) + 0.20\,(0,2) + 0.40\,(2,2) = (1.2,\ 1.2)\). All rows:
\[
O \approx \begin{pmatrix} 1.20 & 1.20 \\ 1.00 & 1.60 \\ 1.26 & 1.50 \end{pmatrix}
\]
Things to notice:

Every row of \(A\) sums to 1, so each output is a genuine weighted average of the value vectors.
Token 3 has the query \((1,1)\), which has a positive dot product with every key, and its largest weight (0.50) is on itself because its own key \((1,1)\) matches best.
The output has the same number of rows as the input (\(n\)): attention maps a sequence of \(n\) vectors to a sequence of \(n\) vectors.

title: Scaled Dot-Product Attention, Step by Step
text:
Why divide by \(\sqrt{d_k}\)?
The paper’s explanation (Vaswani et al., 2017) is that for large \(d_k\) the dot products grow large in magnitude, which pushes softmax into regions where its gradients are extremely small. The authors present this explicitly as a suspicion rather than a proven result, supported by the observation that, without scaling, dot-product attention did worse than additive attention at larger \(d_k\) (Britz et al., 2017). Here is the reasoning behind it, in three steps.
Step 1: the size of a dot product grows with \(d_k\). Assume the components of a query \(q\) and a key \(k\) are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1. Then each product \(q_i k_i\) has mean 0 and variance 1. The dot product \(q \cdot k = \sum_{i=1}^{d_k} q_i k_i\) adds up \(d_k\) independent terms, and variances of independent terms add:
\[
\text{Var}(q \cdot k) = d_k \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \text{standard deviation} = \sqrt{d_k}
\]
So with \(d_k = 64\), typical scores are spread over a range of about \(\pm 8\), not \(\pm 1\). (This assumption is a clean idealization, roughly right for freshly initialized vectors; it is the argument’s starting point, not a guarantee during training.)
Step 2: big scores make softmax nearly one-hot. Softmax exponentiates its inputs, so a gap of 8 between two scores means a weight ratio of \(e^8 \approx 3000\). One key grabs almost all the weight. We can check this numerically with random vectors:
import numpy as np

def softmax(z, axis=-1):
    z = z - z.max(axis=axis, keepdims=True)
    e = np.exp(z)
    return e / e.sum(axis=axis, keepdims=True)

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
d_k = 64

# 1) variance of a dot product grows with d_k
q = rng.standard_normal((100_000, d_k))
k = rng.standard_normal((100_000, d_k))
s = (q * k).sum(axis=1)
print(s.var(), s.std(), (s / np.sqrt(d_k)).std())   # 64.0  8.0  1.0

# 2) softmax saturation: 8 random keys per query
q = rng.standard_normal((1000, d_k))
K8 = rng.standard_normal((1000, 8, d_k))
s = np.einsum("bd,bnd->bn", q, K8)
print(softmax(s).max(axis=1).mean())                  # 0.88  (unscaled)
print(softmax(s / np.sqrt(d_k)).max(axis=1).mean())   # 0.36  (scaled)

# 3) size of the softmax derivatives, J_ij = p_i (delta_ij - p_j)
def mean_abs_jacobian(p):
    J = p[:, :, None] * np.eye(8) - p[:, :, None] * p[:, None, :]
    return np.abs(J).mean()
print(mean_abs_jacobian(softmax(s)))                  # ~0.005 (unscaled)
print(mean_abs_jacobian(softmax(s / np.sqrt(d_k))))   # ~0.024 (scaled)
Without scaling, the largest of 8 weights is on average 0.88 (almost one-hot). With scaling it is 0.36, a much softer distribution.
Step 3: a near-one-hot softmax has almost no gradient. For softmax outputs \(p\), the derivative of output \(p_i\) with respect to input \(s_j\) is \(p_i(\delta_{ij} - p_j)\), where \(\delta_{ij}\) is 1 if \(i = j\) and 0 otherwise. If \(p\) is nearly one-hot, then for every \(i\) either \(p_i \approx 0\) or \(1 - p_i \approx 0\), so these derivatives all shrink toward zero. Learning stalls for that attention row. In the same simulation, the average size of a derivative entry is roughly 0.005 without scaling versus 0.024 with it, about 4 to 5 times smaller.
Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) rescales the variance of the scores back to 1, whatever \(d_k\) is. That is the whole trick.

title: Scaled Dot-Product Attention, Step by Step
text:
Why attention instead of recurrence?
The paper motivates self-attention with three desiderata: computation per layer, how much can run in parallel, and how short the path is between two distant positions (Vaswani et al., 2017). Their comparison (restated here), with \(n\) = sequence length, \(d\) = representation size, \(k\) = convolution kernel size:









Layer type
Computation per layer
Sequential operations
Longest path between two positions




Self-attention
\(O(n^2 \cdot d)\)
\(O(1)\)
\(O(1)\)


Recurrent
\(O(n \cdot d^2)\)
\(O(n)\)
\(O(n)\)


Convolutional
\(O(k \cdot n \cdot d^2)\)
\(O(1)\)
\(O(\log_k n)\)



In plain words:

Sequential operations. A recurrent layer must process position 1, then 2, then 3, and so on, so it cannot parallelize across the sequence. Attention computes all positions at once as matrix multiplications, which is what GPUs are good at.
Path length. In a recurrent network, a signal from token 1 must pass through \(n-1\) steps to reach token \(n\), and learning long-range dependencies is hard along such paths. In attention every pair of tokens is directly connected.
Cost. Attention is cheaper per layer than recurrence when \(n < d\), which the paper notes is typical for sentence representations. When \(n\) gets large the \(n^2\) term hurts. That cost is the subject of Part 7.

title: Scaled Dot-Product Attention, Step by Step
text:
A minimal implementation
import numpy as np

def softmax(z, axis=-1):
    z = z - z.max(axis=axis, keepdims=True)      # subtract the max for numerical stability
    e = np.exp(z)
    return e / e.sum(axis=axis, keepdims=True)

def attention(Q, K, V):
    d_k = Q.shape[-1]
    scores = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(d_k)              # (n, n)
    weights = softmax(scores, axis=-1)           # each row sums to 1
    return weights @ V, weights                  # (n, d_v), (n, n)

Q = K = np.array([[1., 0.], [0., 1.], [1., 1.]])
V = np.array([[1., 0.], [0., 2.], [2., 2.]])
out, w = attention(Q, K, V)
print(np.round(w, 2))     # [[0.4  0.2  0.4 ] [0.2  0.4  0.4 ] [0.25 0.25 0.5 ]]
print(np.round(out, 2))   # [[1.2  1.2 ] [1.   1.6 ] [1.26 1.5 ]]
This reproduces the worked example. In a real model \(Q\), \(K\) and \(V\) come from \(XW^Q\), \(XW^K\), \(XW^V\) with learned weights, and many such operations run in parallel (next articles).

title: Scaled Dot-Product Attention, Step by Step
section: What this operation does not do yet
text:
What this operation does not do yet

It has no sense of order. If you shuffle the rows of \(X\), the rows of the output are shuffled in exactly the same way. Attention alone cannot tell “dog bites man” from “man bites dog”, so Transformers add positional information to the embeddings. That is the topic of a later article in this series.
It looks at every token, including the future. For text generation, a token must not see the tokens that come after it. That needs a mask, covered in the Part 5.
It produces one weighted average per token. Multi-head attention runs several of these in parallel, each with its own projections. See Part 6.

title: Scaled Dot-Product Attention, Step by Step
text:
Common pitfalls

Softmax over the wrong axis. Softmax is applied along each row of \(S\) (over the keys), so every query’s weights sum to 1. The columns do not sum to 1.
Dividing by \(d_k\) instead of \(\sqrt{d_k}\), or forgetting the scaling altogether. The model may still train, but the saturation problem above gets worse as \(d_k\) grows.
Skipping numerical stabilization. Exponentiating large scores overflows, especially in 16-bit floats. Subtracting the row maximum before exp does not change the result and prevents it.
Mismatched dimensions. Queries and keys must have the same size \(d_k\) (they are dotted together). Values can have a different size \(d_v\); the output has \(d_v\) columns.
Reading attention maps as explanations. It is tempting to say “the model predicted this because it attended to that word”. Studies of attention in NLP models found that attention weights often do not correlate with other measures of feature importance, and that very different attention patterns can give the same prediction (Jain & Wallace, 2019). The original paper’s own attention visualizations are presented in hedged terms: some heads apparently track sentence structure (Vaswani et al., 2017). Treat attention maps as a window onto the computation, not as a proof of reasoning.
Confusing the cost of the matrix with the cost of the layer. \(S\) and \(A\) are \(n \times n\) per head per layer. For short inputs this is nothing; for long contexts it dominates.

title: Scaled Dot-Product Attention, Step by Step
text:
Summary

Attention gives every token a new vector: a weighted average of all tokens’ values, with weights from how well its query matches their keys.
Shapes: \(Q, K \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_k}\), \(V \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_v}\), scores and weights are \(n \times n\), output is \(n \times d_v\).
Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) keeps the score variance at 1, which keeps softmax away from saturation where gradients vanish.
Compared with recurrence, attention parallelizes across positions and connects any two tokens in one step, at an \(O(n^2 \cdot d)\) cost per layer.

title: Multi-Head Attention: Several Views of the Same Sequence
text: This is Part 6, the third of four articles on attention. We have scaled dot-product attention and we know how to mask it and use it across an encoder and a decoder. Now we answer a natural question: why does every real Transformer run attention several times in parallel rather than once?

title: Multi-Head Attention: Several Views of the Same Sequence
section: Why one attention is not enough
text:
Why one attention is not enough
A single attention operation gives each token one softmax distribution and therefore one weighted average of the value vectors. That average has to serve every purpose at once. Consider the word “it” in a sentence. To build a good representation, the model may want to look at the noun that “it” refers to, at the verb it is the subject of, and at a nearby punctuation mark, and these are different questions that deserve different weightings.
The original paper puts the problem this way: with a single head, averaging inhibits the model’s ability to attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions (Vaswani et al., 2017). The same paper notes that self-attention relates any two positions in a constant number of operations, at the price of reduced effective resolution because attention-weighted positions are averaged, and that multi-head attention is what counteracts this effect.
The idea of multi-head attention: run \(h\) smaller attentions in parallel, each with its own learned projections (its own notion of “query”, “key” and “value”), then concatenate their results and mix them with one more projection.

title: Multi-Head Attention: Several Views of the Same Sequence
text:
The formulas
For head \(i \in \{1, \dots, h\}\):
\[
\text{head}_i = \text{Attention}\big(X W_i^Q,\; X W_i^K,\; X W_i^V\big),
\qquad
\text{MultiHead}(X) = \text{Concat}(\text{head}_1, \dots, \text{head}_h)\, W^O
\]
(In self-attention the queries, keys and values all start from the same input \(X\). In cross-attention the keys and values start from the encoder output instead.)

Follow the shapes with \(d_\text{model} = 512\) and \(h = 8\):

Each head projects \(X\) (\(n \times 512\)) down to \(n \times 64\) queries, keys and values.
Each head computes its own \(n \times n\) attention weights and produces an \(n \times 64\) output.
Concatenating 8 outputs of width 64 gives \(n \times 512\) again.
\(W^O\) (\(512 \times 512\)) mixes the heads’ outputs, giving the layer’s final \(n \times 512\) output.

The output has the same shape as the input, so layers can be stacked.

title: Multi-Head Attention: Several Views of the Same Sequence
section: Why the cost stays the same
text:
Why the cost stays the same
It is natural to assume 8 heads cost 8 times as much. They do not, because each head works in a space \(h\) times smaller. The paper states that, due to the reduced dimension of each head, the total computational cost is similar to single-head attention with full dimensionality (Vaswani et al., 2017). Here is the arithmetic.
Parameters. One head has three projections of \(512 \times 64\), i.e. \(3 \cdot 512 \cdot 64 = 98{,}304\) weights. Eight heads: \(786{,}432\). Add \(W^O\) (\(512 \times 512 = 262{,}144\)) for a total of \(1{,}048{,}576 = 4 \cdot 512^2\). A single full-width head would use three \(512 \times 512\) matrices plus the same output matrix: exactly the same count.
Compute. Computing the scores \(QK^\top\) for one head costs about \(n^2 \cdot d_k\) multiply-adds. For \(h\) heads that is \(n^2 \cdot h \cdot d_k = n^2 \cdot d_\text{model}\), the same as one full-width head (\(d_k = d_\text{model}\)).
So multi-head attention does not add capacity. It partitions the same width into \(h\) independent subspaces, each with its own softmax. One thing does grow: there are now \(h\) separate \(n \times n\) weight matrices to hold in memory, which is part of why attention memory becomes a problem for long sequences (see the Part 7).

The paper’s reading: single-head attention is 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting, and quality also drops with too many heads; reducing the key size \(d_k\) hurts, which the authors take to suggest that judging compatibility is not easy and a more sophisticated compatibility function than a dot product might help.
Two cautions when quoting these numbers. They come from one translation task and one model size, and the table reports single runs with no variance, so differences of a few tenths of a BLEU point are hard to interpret. The solid message is the larger one: one wide head is clearly worse than a moderate number of narrower heads, and there is a sweet spot rather than “more is always better”.

title: Multi-Head Attention: Several Views of the Same Sequence
text:
What do heads actually learn?
The paper’s appendix visualizes attention weights from layer 5 of 6 in the encoder. The authors describe many heads as attending to a long-distance dependency (the verb “making” attending to “more difficult”), two heads as “apparently involved in anaphora resolution” (the word “its” pointing back at “Law” and “application”), and others as showing behaviour that appears related to sentence structure, concluding that different heads learned different tasks (Vaswani et al., 2017). These are hand-picked qualitative examples from one layer of one model, and the wording is deliberately hedged.
Later work gives a more detailed picture, in translation models:

Voita et al. (2019) found that a small number of heads with identifiable roles (attending to adjacent positions, to syntactic relations, or to rare words) did most of the work, and that most of the other heads could be pruned with little loss in quality.
Michel et al. (2019) found that a large share of heads can be removed at test time without significantly hurting performance, and that some layers can even be reduced to a single head. They also found that the encoder-decoder (cross) attention layers depend more on having multiple heads than self-attention layers do.

So “different heads learn different things” has real support, but so does “many heads are redundant”. Both facts are consistent with the heads being a flexible budget rather than a set of hand-designed experts.

title: Multi-Head Attention: Several Views of the Same Sequence
text:
Common pitfalls

\(d_\text{model}\) must be divisible by \(h\). Otherwise \(d_k = d_\text{model}/h\) is not an integer and the reshape fails.
Forgetting the output projection \(W^O\). Concatenation alone leaves the heads’ outputs side by side. \(W^O\) is what mixes information across heads.
Assuming more heads is better. In the paper’s own ablation, 32 heads scored below 8 and 16. More heads also means a smaller \(d_k\) per head.
Thinking heads add parameters or compute. At fixed \(d_\text{model}\) the parameter count and the score computation are unchanged, as computed above. What grows is the number of \(n \times n\) weight matrices.
Over-reading single-head visualizations. A head that looks like it tracks grammar in one example, in one layer, may behave differently elsewhere, and attention weights alone are not a faithful explanation of a model’s output. See the pitfalls in the Part 4.
Applying the mask per head by mistake. The same causal mask is shared by all heads; an \((n, n)\) mask broadcasts across the head dimension.

title: Multi-Head Attention: Several Views of the Same Sequence
text:
Summary

Multi-head attention runs \(h\) attentions in parallel, each in a \(d_k = d_\text{model}/h\) dimensional subspace, then concatenates and mixes them with \(W^O\).
Parameters and score computation match one full-width head; the number of attention matrices is \(h\) times larger.
In the original ablations, one head was 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting, and too many heads also hurt.
Heads show some specialization, but studies of trained translation models find many heads are removable.

title: Companion: Where the Rotation Comes From, and the Decay Bound
text: This page backs up Part 9. It re-derives two results from the RoFormer paper (Su et al., 2021, Sections 3.4.1 and 3.4.3) and spells out which steps are forced and which are choices.

title: Companion: Where the Rotation Comes From, and the Decay Bound
text:
1. Setting up the 2D problem
Identify a 2D vector \((a,b)\in\mathbb{R}^2\) with the complex number \(a+\mathrm{i}b\). For complex \(u,v\) the usual dot product of the corresponding 2D vectors is \(\mathrm{Re}(u\bar v)\), where \(\bar v\) is the complex conjugate.
Let \(q = W_q x_m\) and \(k = W_k x_n\) be the content-only query and key (complex numbers), and let \(f_q(x_m,m)\), \(f_k(x_n,n)\) be the position-aware versions. We require:

(Initial condition) with no position, nothing changes: \(q=f_q(x_m,0)=W_q x_m\) and \(k=f_k(x_n,0)=W_k x_n\).
(Relative-only) the complex product \(f_q(x_m,m)\,\overline{f_k(x_n,n)}\) depends on the positions only through \(m-n\): it equals some function \(G(x_m,x_n,m-n)\). Its real part is the dot product we care about. (Asking for the whole complex product to be relative-only is slightly stronger than asking for its real part to be, and it is what the paper does.)

Write everything in polar form, \(f_q = r_q e^{\mathrm{i}\alpha_q}\), \(f_k = r_k e^{\mathrm{i}\alpha_k}\), \(G = r_G e^{\mathrm{i}\alpha_G}\), where \(r\) is a length and \(\alpha\) an angle. The product condition splits into a statement about lengths and a statement about angles:
\[
r_q(x_m,m)\,r_k(x_n,n) = r_G(x_m,x_n,m-n), \qquad
\alpha_q(x_m,m)-\alpha_k(x_n,n) = \alpha_G(x_m,x_n,m-n) \tag{1}
\]
The initial condition specifies that at position \(0\), the functions reduce to the base content projections. If we express the base queries and keys in polar form as \(q = \|q\|e^{\mathrm{i}\varphi_q}\) and \(k = \|k\|e^{\mathrm{i}\varphi_k}\), equating them to our position-aware functions at \(m=0\) and \(n=0\) explicitly pins down the initial radii and angles:
\[
r_q(x_m,0) = \|q\|, \qquad r_k(x_n,0) = \|k\|
\] \[
\alpha_q(x_m,0) = \varphi_q, \qquad \alpha_k(x_n,0) = \varphi_k \tag{2}
\]

title: Companion: Where the Rotation Comes From, and the Decay Bound
text:
2. Solving it
Set \(m=n\). Then \(m-n=0\), so the right-hand sides of (1) no longer depend on the position:
\[
r_q(x_m,m)\,r_k(x_n,m) = r_G(x_m,x_n,0) = r_q(x_m,0)\,r_k(x_n,0) = \|q\|\|k\|
\] \[
\alpha_q(x_m,m)-\alpha_k(x_n,m) = \alpha_G(x_m,x_n,0) = \varphi_q-\varphi_k
\]
Lengths. The first equation only fixes the product of the two radii. The simplest solution, and the one the paper takes, keeps each radius at its position-0 value: \(r_q(x_m,m)=\|q\|\) and \(r_k(x_n,n)=\|k\|\). This is a choice, but a natural one, because a pure rotation never changes lengths.
Angles. The second equation says \(\alpha_q(x_m,m)-\varphi_q = \alpha_k(x_n,m)-\varphi_k\). Because the content vectors \(x_m\) and \(x_n\) are independent of each other, this equality demonstrates that for a fixed position \(m\), the difference between the position-aware angle and the base content angle is identical for all query and key vectors, regardless of their content. We can therefore define this common, position-dependent shift as \(\phi(m)\). So the position shifts every angle by the same position-only amount: \(\alpha_q = \varphi_q + \phi(m)\) and \(\alpha_k=\varphi_k+\phi(n)\). The initial condition gives \(\phi(0)=0\).
Pin down \(\phi\). Plug these into the angle part of (1) with \(n=m-1\):
\[
\phi(m)-\phi(m-1) = \alpha_G(x_m,x_{m-1},1)-\varphi_q+\varphi_k
\]
The right-hand side does not depend on the position \(m\), so \(\phi\) increases by the same constant each step. Call that constant \(\theta\). An integer sequence with constant increments is an arithmetic progression, and with \(\phi(0)=0\):
\[
\phi(m) = m\theta
\]
(\(\theta=0\) would mean no position information at all, so \(\theta\neq 0\).)
Result.
\[
f_q(x_m,m) = (W_q x_m)\,e^{\mathrm{i}m\theta},\qquad
f_k(x_n,n) = (W_k x_n)\,e^{\mathrm{i}n\theta},\qquad
\mathrm{Re}\!\left[f_q\overline{f_k}\right]=\mathrm{Re}\!\left[(W_qx_m)\overline{(W_kx_n)}\,e^{\mathrm{i}(m-n)\theta}\right]
\]
Multiplying by \(e^{\mathrm{i}m\theta}\) is a rotation by \(m\theta\), which is the matrix form used in Part 9.
What was assumed. This is a solution, not the only one: it relies on the initial condition, on the stronger complex form of the relative-only requirement, and on the choice of position-independent radii. In \(d\) dimensions the paper applies the 2D solution to each of the \(d/2\) pairs separately and picks the frequencies \(\theta_i=10000^{-2i/d}\) following the sinusoidal encoding. That choice is motivated by tradition and by the decay property below, not derived from the requirement.

title: Companion: Where the Rotation Comes From, and the Decay Bound
text:
3. The long-term decay bound
In \(d\) dimensions, group the entries of \(q=W_qx_m\) and \(k=W_kx_n\) into \(d/2\) complex pairs \(q_i,k_i\in\mathbb{C}\) (\(i=0,\dots,d/2-1\)). With \(\Delta=m-n\), the RoPE score is
\[
\tilde q_m^\top\tilde k_n = \mathrm{Re}\Big[\sum_{i=0}^{d/2-1} h_i\,e^{\mathrm{i}\Delta\theta_i}\Big],\qquad h_i = q_i\overline{k_i}
\]
where, \(q_m = f_q(x_m, m)\) and \(k_n = f_k(x_n, n)\)
Define the partial sums \(S_j = \sum_{i=0}^{j-1}e^{\mathrm{i}\Delta\theta_i}\), and let \(S_0=0\) and \(h_{d/2}=0\). By simply expanding the products and regrouping the terms to shift the difference from the \(S\) terms to the \(h\) terms (a technique known as Abel summation) we get:
\[
\sum_{i=0}^{d/2-1}h_i\,(S_{i+1}-S_i) \;=\; -\sum_{i=0}^{d/2-1}S_{i+1}\,(h_{i+1}-h_i)
\]
The LHS is exactly the score sum, since \(e^{\mathrm{i}\Delta\theta_i}=S_{i+1}-S_i\). Taking absolute values and using the triangle inequality:
\[
\Big|\sum_i h_i e^{\mathrm{i}\Delta\theta_i}\Big|
\le \sum_i |S_{i+1}|\,|h_{i+1}-h_i|
\le \Big(\max_i |h_{i+1}-h_i|\Big)\sum_{i=0}^{d/2-1}|S_{i+1}|
\]
So the score is bounded by (how much the pair products \(h_i\) vary from pair to pair) times \(\sum_j|S_j|\). The first factor depends on the particular \(q\) and \(k\). The second depends only on the distance \(\Delta\) and the frequencies. The paper’s claim is that the average \(\frac{2}{d}\sum_j|S_j|\) shrinks as \(|\Delta|\) grows when \(\theta_i=10000^{-2i/d}\), and it shows this in a plot.

3.1 Why the Bound Shrinks with Distance
At \(\Delta=0\), all terms \(e^{\mathrm{i}\Delta\theta_i}\) equal \(1\). This means the partial sums are simply \(|S_j|=j\), and their average across all dimensions is exactly \((d/2+1)/2\).
To understand why this average drops as \(\Delta\) grows, shift perspective and treat \(\theta\) as a continuous variable, looking at the terms \(e^{\mathrm{i}\Delta\theta}\). In this \(\theta\)-space, the function oscillates with a period of \(2\pi/\Delta\).
The base frequencies \(\theta_i = 10000^{-2i/d}\) span a range from \(1\) down to \(0.0001\). As the relative distance \(\Delta\) increases, the period \(2\pi/\Delta\) shrinks rapidly. This forces the function to oscillate many times across the available \(\theta\) range. When you sum over these highly oscillatory complex values, the vectors point in all different directions around the unit circle and largely cancel each other out through destructive interference.
However, this is an intuitive heuristic rather than a conclusive mathematical proof. If this were a continuous integration over a uniform range (\(\int e^{\mathrm{i}\Delta\theta} d\theta\)), the cancellations would be clean and the value would decay smoothly toward zero. But RoPE computes a discrete sum over exponentially spaced points. This non-uniform sampling means the cancellation is imperfect, which is probably why the sum doesn’t perfectly decay to zero, but instead hits a messy, oscillating plateau.
Here is our plot of the average for \(d=128\):



Average partial-sum magnitude versus relative distance. It falls from \(32.5\) at \(\Delta=0\) to between about \(6.4\) and \(11.6\) over the range \(100\le\Delta\le 256\), oscillating as it goes.




3.2 Caveats and What the Bound Actually Means
This result describes a trend in an upper bound, not a strict guarantee about actual attention scores. When interpreting this decay, keep three limitations in mind:

The bound is data-dependent. The upper bound is a product of the distance factor \(\sum_i |S_{i+1}|\) and a content-dependent factor \(\max_i |h_{i+1}-h_i|\), which is governed by the input tokens and the learned weights \(W_q, W_k\). If the pairwise products \(h_i\) vary sharply from one pair to the next, that maximum difference can easily overpower the shrinking distance factor.
The plateau never reaches zero. Like the plot showed, the distance term drops from \(32.5\) down to a floor of roughly \(6.4\) to \(11.6\), and then just oscillates. Because the bound never asymptotes to \(0\), RoPE inherently cannot force distant tokens to have a zero attention score. It only applies a mild, structural suppression.
Trained models can concentrate energy in the slow pairs. Because different dimension pairs rotate at vastly different speeds, a trained model can bypass the decay entirely by routing long-range information into the slowest-rotating dimensions.



3.3 How Models Bypass Decay: Concentrating Energy in Slow Pairs
To see how a model circumvents the decay bound in practice, look at how the full \(d\)-dimensional dot product is assembled from individual 2D pairs.
RoPE partitions the \(d\) coordinates of \(q = W_q x_m\) and \(k = W_k x_n\) into \(d/2\) disjoint 2D pairs: \((0,1), (2,3), \dots, (d-2, d-1)\). Let \(q^{(i)}, k^{(i)} \in \mathbb{R}^2\) be the \(i\)-th pair before rotation, with lengths \(\|q^{(i)}\|, \|k^{(i)}\|\) and an initial content angle \(\psi_i = \varphi_q^{(i)} - \varphi_k^{(i)}\) between them.
When RoPE rotates \(q^{(i)}\) by \(m\theta_i\) and \(k^{(i)}\) by \(n\theta_i\), their lengths stay fixed while the angle between them shifts by \((m-n)\theta_i = \Delta\theta_i\). Summing the standard 2D dot products across all \(d/2\) pairs gives the full RoPE attention score:
\[
\tilde{q}_m^\top \tilde{k}_n = \sum_{i=0}^{d/2-1} \|q^{(i)}\| \|k^{(i)}\| \cos(\psi_i + \Delta\theta_i)
\]
Each term in this sum has two distinct components:

The pair magnitude \(\|q^{(i)}\| \|k^{(i)}\|\) (“energy”): How large the numbers are in pair \(i\). This acts as a volume knob controlling how much pair \(i\) contributes to the total attention score, and it is controlled entirely by rows \(2i\) and \(2i+1\) of the learned matrices \(W_q\) and \(W_k\).
The rotation factor \(\cos(\psi_i + \Delta\theta_i)\): How aligned the pair remains after being twisted across distance \(\Delta\) at frequency \(\theta_i = 10000^{-2i/d}\).

Because \(\theta_i\) decays exponentially with \(i\), the early pairs and late pairs behave completely differently over long distances:

Fast pairs (small \(i\)): Pair \(i=0\) has \(\theta_0 = 1\text{ rad/token}\) (\(\approx 57.3^\circ\text{/token}\)), completing a full rotation every \(\lambda_0 = 2\pi \approx 6.28\) tokens. Over long distances like \(\Delta = 2000\), \(\cos(\Delta\theta_0)\) oscillates wildly between \(+1\) and \(-1\), turning the pair’s contribution into high-frequency noise.
Slow pairs (large \(i\)): A late pair with a wavelength of \(\lambda_i = 60,000\) tokens has \(\theta_i = 2\pi / 60,000\). Even across a distance of \(\Delta = 2000\) tokens, the vector rotates by only \(\Delta\theta_i = \pi/15\text{ rad} = 12^\circ\). Since \(\cos(12^\circ) \approx 0.978\), nearly \(98\%\) of the aligned dot product survives intact.


3.3.1 A Concrete \(d=4\) Example
Suppose \(d=4\), giving just two pairs: Pair \(0\) (fast) and Pair \(1\) (slow, with \(\Delta\theta_1 = 12^\circ\) at \(\Delta = 2000\)). Suppose a pronoun at position \(m=2000\) needs to attend strongly to a noun at \(n=0\) (\(\Delta = 2000\)), and the content projections are perfectly aligned in both pairs (\(\psi_0 = \psi_1 = 0\)).

Case A (Equal energy across pairs): Suppose \(W_q\) and \(W_k\) assign unit length to both pairs, \(q = k = [1, 0, \; 1, 0]\). Both pairs have \(\|q^{(i)}\|\|k^{(i)}\| = 1\), and the unrotated dot product (\(\Delta=0\)) is \(1 + 1 = 2\). At \(\Delta = 2000\), the fast pair spins to some arbitrary value—say \(\cos(2000\theta_0) \approx -0.8\)—while the slow pair stays near \(\cos(12^\circ) \approx 0.98\). The total score drops to: \[
\tilde{q}_m^\top \tilde{k}_n = (1 \times -0.8) + (1 \times 0.98) = 0.18
\]
Case B (Energy concentrated in the slow pair): During training, gradient descent is penalized if the model fails to connect the pronoun to the distant noun. To prevent the fast pair from corrupting the long-range score, the optimizer can update \(W_q\) and \(W_k\) to zero out rows \(0,1\) and scale up rows \(2,3\), producing \(q = k = [0, 0, \; \sqrt{2}, 0]\). The total vector norm is unchanged (\(\|q\| = \|k\| = \sqrt{2}\)), and the \(\Delta=0\) score is still \(2\). Now, at \(\Delta = 2000\), the fast pair’s wild rotation is multiplied by zero magnitude, while the slow pair carries all the weight: \[
\tilde{q}_m^\top \tilde{k}_n = (0 \times -0.8) + (2 \times 0.98) = 1.96
\]

In terms of the Abel summation bound, setting \(h_0 = 0\) and \(h_1 = 2\) eliminates the cancellation between pairs and inflates the data-dependent factor \(\max_i |h_{i+1}-h_i|\). In practice, trained transformers naturally learn this division of labor: they use fast-rotating pairs to attend to local syntax and immediate neighbors, while routing long-range semantic dependencies into slow-rotating pairs where RoPE’s decay is too weak to erase them.
As the RoFormer authors note in their limitations section, while the decay bound provides useful intuition for why uniformly distributed features fade with distance, there is still no complete theoretical explanation for why RoPE empirically outperforms other position encodings on long texts.
How to read this. It is a trend in an upper bound, not a guarantee about actual attention. The bound has a data-dependent factor (\(|h_{i+1}-h_i|\)), the plateau does not go to zero, and a trained model can put its query and key energy in the slow pairs (small \(\theta_i\)) where this decay is weak. The paper’s limitations section also notes that the authors have no faithful explanation of why RoPE does better on long texts than other methods.

title: Stretching RoPE to Long Contexts
text: A model trained on 4,096-token sequences is asked to read 32,000 tokens. Part 9 showed that RoPE is relative, so you might hope this just works. It does not. This article explains why, and walks through the main fixes: position interpolation (PI), NTK-aware scaling, dynamic scaling, NTK-by-parts and YaRN. It then covers what else a long-context model needs, and why a big context window does not guarantee the model uses it well.

title: Stretching RoPE to Long Contexts
section: 1. Why plain RoPE fails beyond the training length
text:
1. Why plain RoPE fails beyond the training length
Recall from Part 9 that pair \(i\) of a query or key is rotated by \(m\theta_i\) at position \(m\), with \(\theta_i = 10000^{-2i/d}\) and \(i=0,\dots,d/2-1\). Its wavelength is \(\lambda_i = 2\pi/\theta_i\), the number of tokens per full turn. Let \(L\) be the training length.

Fast pairs (\(\lambda_i \ll L\)) complete many turns during training, so they have seen every angle many times. Positions beyond \(L\) just revisit familiar angles.
Slow pairs (\(\lambda_i > L\)) never complete a turn during training. They have only ever seen a partial arc of angles. Beyond position \(L\) they enter angles the network has never encountered.

For a head dimension \(d=128\) and \(L=4096\), \(18\) of the \(64\) pairs are slow in this sense. The YaRN authors point out that this makes RoPE less purely “relative” than it looks: a slow pair behaves like an absolute position marker within the training range, and out-of-range values are out of distribution. The position interpolation paper describes the symptom: direct extrapolation can produce catastrophically large attention scores that ruin self-attention.
Notation used below: \(L\) is the training length, \(L'>L\) the target length, and \(s = L'/L\) the scale factor. \(\theta_i\) and \(\lambda_i=2\pi/\theta_i\) are as above, and \(b=10000\) is the base of \(\theta_i = b^{-2i/d}\).



RoPE wavelength of each pair for \(d=128\), \(s=8\), \(L=4096\), under different scaling methods (our own computation). Where a method equals PI the curves coincide.

title: Stretching RoPE to Long Contexts
text:
2. The methods





flowchart LR
  A["<b>RoPE</b><br/>θᵢ = b^(−2i/d)"] --> B["<b>Position interpolation</b><br/>m → m / s"]
  B --> C["<b>NTK-aware</b><br/>b → b · s^(d/(d−2))"]
  C --> D["<b>Dynamic scaling</b><br/>s = max(1, l′/L)"]
  C --> E["<b>NTK-by-parts</b><br/>blend θᵢ and θᵢ/s per pair"]
  E --> F["<b>YaRN</b><br/>NTK-by-parts + attention scale"]






All of them modify the angle \(m\theta_i\) that pair \(i\) is rotated by. In the YaRN paper’s unified notation, a method replaces the position \(m\) by some \(g(m)\) and the frequencies \(\theta_i\) by some \(h(\theta_i)\).

Position interpolation (PI)
Chen et al. (2023) (and concurrently the blogger kaiokendev) squeeze the new, longer range of positions back into the trained range:
\[
m \;\to\; \frac{m}{s} = \frac{mL}{L'} .
\]
Equivalently, every \(\theta_i\) becomes \(\theta_i/s\), so every wavelength gets \(s\) times longer. The largest position \(L'\) now produces the same angles as position \(L\) did in training, so no pair meets an unseen angle. The paper shows the interpolated attention score has a much smaller upper bound than the extrapolated one (about 600 times smaller in their LLaMA 7B setting) and extends LLaMA models to 32,768 tokens with fine-tuning of about 1,000 steps.
The cost: resolution. Adjacent tokens used to be one radian apart on the fastest pair. Now they are \(1/s\) radians apart, so the fast pairs have trouble telling neighbours apart. The YaRN authors report that PI fine-tunes of that period degraded at roughly \(s=8\) and above.


NTK-aware scaling
Instead of stretching every pair equally, change the base: \(b \to b' = b\cdot s^{\,d/(d-2)}\). Then
\[
\theta'_i = b'^{-2i/d} = \theta_i \cdot s^{-2i/(d-2)} .
\]
Check the two ends. For \(i=0\) the factor is \(1\): the fastest pair is untouched. For the last pair, \(i=d/2-1\), the exponent is \(-1\): the slowest pair is divided by exactly \(s\), as in PI. In between the stretch grows smoothly. So high frequencies (local detail) are kept and low frequencies (long range) are stretched. This was introduced by the pseudonymous user bloc97 in a 2023 forum post (the name refers to Neural Tangent Kernel results about learning high-frequency functions; it is a heuristic motivation), and documented in the YaRN paper. Code Llama used the same idea by setting the base to 1,000,000.
Limits: the method works reasonably without fine-tuning, but it slightly extrapolates some pairs, so the real extension is not exactly \(s\), and fine-tuning with it gave worse results than PI in the YaRN paper’s analysis. The best base is usually found empirically.


Dynamic scaling (“Dynamic NTK”)
Rather than fixing \(s=L'/L\) for all inputs, recompute it from the current length \(l'\) at each forward pass:
\[
s = \max\!\left(1, \frac{l'}{L}\right).
\]
Short inputs are untouched (no loss below \(L\)), and the model degrades gradually when the length grows instead of failing abruptly at \(L'\). It works well on models that were never fine-tuned for longer contexts. KV-cache consequence: since the rotation of every past token changes whenever \(s\) changes, the cache must store keys before RoPE and apply the rotation at attention time.


NTK-by-parts
The YaRN paper’s refinement looks at each pair’s wavelength relative to the training length. Let \(r_i = L/\lambda_i\) be the number of full turns pair \(i\) completes within \(L\) tokens, and let \(\alpha<\beta\) be two thresholds. The ramp is
\[
\gamma(r) = \begin{cases} 0 & r<\alpha \\ \dfrac{r-\alpha}{\beta-\alpha} & \alpha\le r\le\beta \\ 1 & r>\beta \end{cases},
\qquad
h(\theta_i) = \big(1-\gamma(r_i)\big)\frac{\theta_i}{s} + \gamma(r_i)\,\theta_i .
\]

Pairs with \(r_i<\alpha\) (slow, they never complete a turn) are fully interpolated like PI, so they never extrapolate.
Pairs with \(r_i>\beta\) (fast) are left alone, preserving fine local resolution.
Pairs in between are blended.

The paper found \(\alpha=1\) and \(\beta=32\) work well for the Llama family; they are tuned per model family. In our \(d=128\), \(L=4096\) example: \(18\) pairs are fully interpolated, \(21\) are untouched and \(25\) are blended.


YaRN
YaRN (“Yet another RoPE extensioN”) is NTK-by-parts plus an attention temperature. A longer context means more keys in each softmax, which flattens it (higher entropy). Dividing the logits by a temperature \(t<1\) re-sharpens them. The paper recommends, for the LLaMA and Llama 2 families,
\[
\sqrt{\frac1t} = 0.1\ln(s) + 1,
\]
found by fitting the best-perplexity value across several scale factors without fine-tuning. It is implemented for free by multiplying both \(q\) and \(k\) by \(\sqrt{1/t}\), which is the same as scaling the precomputed RoPE cos and sin tables, so the attention code is unchanged and there is no run-time overhead. For \(s=8\): \(\sqrt{1/t}\approx 1.208\), so the logits (a product of one scaled \(q\) and one scaled \(k\)) are multiplied by about \(1.46\).
Reported results: state-of-the-art context extension after fine-tuning on less than about 0.1% of the original pre-training data, with 10 times fewer tokens and 2.5 times fewer steps than previous methods. Llama 2 7B and 13B were extended to 128K tokens with a few hundred fine-tuning steps (\(s=16\) for 400 steps on 64K-token data, then \(s=32\) for 200 more).

title: Stretching RoPE to Long Contexts
text:
3. Code
import numpy as np

def rope_freqs(d, base=10000.0):
    return base ** (-2.0 * np.arange(d // 2) / d)

def pi_freqs(d, s, base=10000.0):
    return rope_freqs(d, base) / s                          # all pairs stretched by s

def ntk_aware_freqs(d, s, base=10000.0):
    return rope_freqs(d, base * s ** (d / (d - 2)))         # change of base

def ntk_by_parts_freqs(d, s, L, alpha=1.0, beta=32.0, base=10000.0):
    th = rope_freqs(d, base)
    r = L / (2 * np.pi / th)                                # turns completed within L tokens
    gamma = np.clip((r - alpha) / (beta - alpha), 0.0, 1.0) # 0: interpolate, 1: keep
    return (1 - gamma) * th / s + gamma * th

def yarn_scale(s):
    return 0.1 * np.log(s) + 1.0        # = 1/sqrt(t): multiply both q and k by this

d, L, s = 128, 4096, 8
orig = 2 * np.pi / rope_freqs(d)
for name, f in [("PI", pi_freqs(d, s)),
                ("NTK-aware", ntk_aware_freqs(d, s)),
                ("NTK-by-parts", ntk_by_parts_freqs(d, s, L))]:
    w = 2 * np.pi / f
    print(name, "wavelength ratio, fastest/slowest pair:", w[0] / orig[0], w[-1] / orig[-1])
# PI: 8, 8   NTK-aware: 1, 8   NTK-by-parts: 1, 8
print("pairs that never complete a turn in L:", int((orig > L).sum()), "of", d // 2)   # 18 of 64
To use any of these, pass the modified frequencies to the RoPE function from Part 9 (replace rope_freqs(d, base) by the modified array) and, for YaRN, multiply the rotated \(q\) and \(k\) by yarn_scale(s).

title: Stretching RoPE to Long Contexts
section: 4. What else a long-context model needs
text:
4. What else a long-context model needs
Continued training on long data. Adjusting the angles only makes long positions legal. The model still has to learn to use them. The Llama 3 report describes raising the RoPE base frequency to 500,000 and a long-context pre-training stage that increased the context in six stages from 8K to 128K tokens, using about 800B tokens. Fine-tuning recipes such as PI and YaRN are far lighter (hundreds to about a thousand steps) but are working from an already-trained model.
Perplexity is not the whole story. In the YaRN paper’s passkey-retrieval test (find a five-digit number hidden in a long filler text), a model whose perplexity was already rising beyond 100K tokens still retrieved the passkey at 128K. The authors conclude that the lowest perplexity point does not describe the effective context size.
Systems techniques (intuition only). Ring Attention (Liu et al., 2023) splits a very long sequence into blocks spread across devices arranged in a ring; each device keeps its block of queries and passes key-value blocks around the ring while computing attention against each block it receives, overlapping communication with compute. This makes memory per device scale with the block size rather than the full sequence and computes exact attention. Hybrid architectures use cheap local (sliding-window) attention in most layers and full attention only in some, so most of the compute scales with the window size instead of the sequence length.

title: Stretching RoPE to Long Contexts
section: 5. Long context is not long-context use
text:
5. Long context is not long-context use
A model that accepts 1M tokens does not necessarily use all of them. The “lost in the middle” study (Liu et al., 2023) placed the relevant passage at different positions in long inputs and found accuracy highest when it sat at the beginning or the end of the context and lowest when it was in the middle. Using long contexts well takes both positional machinery that keeps working at long range and training on tasks that reward retrieving from far away.

title: Stretching RoPE to Long Contexts
text:
Common pitfalls

Treating \(s\) as the extension you actually get. NTK-aware scaling slightly extrapolates some pairs, so you may have to set \(s\) higher than \(L'/L\).
Serving with a different scaling than the model was adapted with. A model fine-tuned with PI, YaRN or a particular base expects exactly that frequency set at inference.
Leaving out YaRN’s attention scale. It is part of the method, not an optional extra, and the \(0.1\ln s+1\) value was fitted on LLaMA-family models, so treat it as a starting point for other architectures.
Caching rotated keys under dynamic scaling. If \(s\) changes, cached rotated keys become stale. Cache keys before rotation.
Copying \(\alpha=1,\beta=32\) blindly. They were tuned for the Llama family.
Equating context length with usable context. Check retrieval-style tests, not only perplexity, and test with the relevant information in the middle.
Low-precision angles. Large positions times small frequencies need float32 for the cos and sin tables.

title: Foundations of LLMs
text:
The first series on this site. It covers the foundations of large language models, following the first chapter of The Hitchhiker’s Guide to Agentic AI. New parts are added as I work through the chapter.
Prerequisites: some Python, and basic linear algebra (vectors, matrix products, eigenvalues). The companion pages linked from each article go deeper into the math and can be skipped on a first read.










Part



Title



Description








1


Tokenization and Byte-Pair Encoding: How LLMs Turn Text into Numbers


Why language models don’t read characters or words, how BPE builds a vocabulary by merging frequent pairs, and what that means in practice.






2


From Token IDs to Vectors: How LLMs Embed Text


What the embedding layer actually is, where its vectors come from, how weight tying works, and why the geometry of embeddings matters.






3


Anisotropy and Whitening: Fixing the Geometry of Embeddings


What anisotropy is, what the evidence says about BERT, ELMo and GPT-2, and how whitening (and Whitening-k) reshapes embeddings for similarity search.






4


Scaled Dot-Product Attention, Step by Step


How a token builds a new representation as a weighted mix of all the tokens around it: the intuition, the shapes, a worked example, and the reason for the √d_k scaling.






5


Masks, Cross-Attention and the Original Transformer


The causal mask, teacher forcing and the right shift, cross-attention, and how the original encoder-decoder Transformer became the decoder-only architecture behind modern LLMs.






6


Multi-Head Attention: Several Views of the Same Sequence


How multi-head attention splits one wide attention into several narrower ones, why that costs the same, what the original ablations showed, and how to read claims about what heads learn.






7


The Cost of Attention: n², the KV Cache, GQA and MLA


Where attention’s quadratic cost comes from, what the KV cache is and how big it gets, how GQA and MLA shrink it, and a map of the long-context fixes (FlashAttention, sliding windows, sparse and linear attention, cache eviction).






8


Positional Encoding Basics: Why Transformers Need Positions


Attention has no sense of order. Sinusoidal, learned, relative-bias and ALiBi encodings are four ways to add it.






9


Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE)


RoPE encodes position by rotating queries and keys, so attention scores depend on content and relative distance only. Intuition, math, code.






10


Stretching RoPE to Long Contexts


Why RoPE models break past their training length, and how position interpolation, NTK-aware scaling, dynamic scaling and YaRN fix it. Plus: long context is not the same as long-context use.

title: Tokenization and Byte-Pair Encoding: How LLMs Turn Text into Numbers
text:
A language model never sees text. It sees a sequence of integers. The component that turns text into those integers (and back) is the tokenizer, and its design quietly shapes cost, context length, multilingual quality and even arithmetic ability.
This article covers the one idea behind almost every modern tokenizer, subword tokenization, with Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) as the main example. We build it by hand, implement it in about 40 lines of Python, then look at its cousins (WordPiece, Unigram), the byte-level trick that removes “unknown” tokens, and the special tokens that structure chat prompts.

title: Tokenization and Byte-Pair Encoding: How LLMs Turn Text into Numbers
section: 1. Why not characters, and why not words?
text:
1. Why not characters, and why not words?
Pick a granularity for the pieces (“tokens”) the model reads. There are three obvious options, and two of them fail in opposite directions.

Whole words. The vocabulary must contain every word the model might meet. Real text keeps producing new ones: names, typos, product codes, and in languages like German, compounds such as Abwasserbehandlungsanlage (“sewage water treatment plant”). A word-level model maps anything outside its vocabulary to a single <unk> placeholder and loses the information.
Characters. Nothing is ever unknown, but sequences get long. A transformer’s self-attention compares every position with every other, so its cost grows with \(n^2\), where \(n\) is the sequence length in tokens. Longer sequences also push related pieces of information further apart.
Subwords. Frequent words stay whole; rare words are assembled from smaller pieces the model has seen before.

Sennrich et al. (2016) measured this trade-off on a German training corpus of about 100 million words:

German training corpus statistics, from Sennrich et al. (2016), Table 1.

Characters make the text 5.5× longer, which for a transformer means roughly \(5.5^2 \approx 30\times\) more attention work. Words need a vocabulary 28× bigger than BPE’s. BPE sits in the middle: it turns the same text into only about 12% more tokens than word-level splitting (112M vs 100M), with a vocabulary small enough to fit in an embedding table.

title: Tokenization and Byte-Pair Encoding: How LLMs Turn Text into Numbers
text:
2. BPE by hand
BPE comes from data compression (Gage, 1994): repeatedly replace the most frequent pair of adjacent bytes with a new, unused byte. Sennrich et al. adapted it to words: repeatedly merge the most frequent pair of adjacent symbols into one new symbol.
The learning loop:

Start with a vocabulary of single characters. Write every word in the corpus as a sequence of characters.
Count every adjacent pair of symbols, weighted by how often each word occurs.
Merge the most frequent pair into a new symbol, add it to the vocabulary, and rewrite the corpus.
Repeat steps 2–3 for \(k\) merges.






flowchart LR
    A["Corpus as<br/>characters"] --> B["Count adjacent<br/>pairs (weighted)"]
    B --> C["Pick the most<br/>frequent pair"]
    C --> D["Merge it into a<br/>new symbol"]
    D --> E["Rewrite corpus,<br/>record the merge"]
    E -->|"fewer than k merges"| B
    E -->|"k merges done"| F["Output: base symbols<br/>+ ordered merge list"]







A tiny corpus
Word counts: hug ×10, pug ×5, pun ×12, bun ×4, hugs ×5. The base vocabulary is the seven characters b g h n p s u.
Merge 1. Pair counts: u g = 10 + 5 + 5 = 20, p u = 5 + 12 = 17, u n = 12 + 4 = 16, h u = 15, g s = 5, b u = 4. Winner: u g → ug.
After rewriting, the corpus is h ug ×10, p ug ×5, p u n ×12, b u n ×4, h ug s ×5.
Merge 2. Counts are recomputed on the rewritten corpus. pug is now p ug, so it no longer contributes to p u, which drops from 17 to 12. Now u n = 16 is the top pair → un.
Merge 3. h ug = 10 + 5 = 15 wins → hug.

Merging adds a symbol; it does not remove the old ones. u and g stay in the vocabulary (they still appear on their own in pun and bun). So the final vocabulary is
\[|V| = |V_0| + k\]
where \(|V|\) is the final vocabulary size, \(|V_0|\) is the number of starting symbols (here 7), and \(k\) is the number of merges (here 3), giving 10 symbols. The merge count \(k\) is the algorithm’s only hyperparameter.


Using the merges on new text
Learning produces an ordered list of merges. To tokenize any word, split it into characters, then replay the merges in the order they were learned.





flowchart LR
    W["bugs"] --> S["b · u · g · s"]
    S -->|"merge 1: u+g"| M1["b · ug · s"]
    M1 -->|"merge 2: u+n"| M2["no match"]
    M2 -->|"merge 3: h+ug"| M3["no match"]
    M3 --> R["tokens: b, ug, s"]






bugs never appeared in training, yet it becomes b, ug, s, all known symbols. That is the “open vocabulary” property: any word made of known characters can be encoded.
Two details from the original paper:

Merges never cross word boundaries, so the algorithm runs on a word-frequency dictionary, which is much faster than scanning raw text.
Sennrich et al. added a special end-of-word symbol to each word so the original spacing can be restored after translation. Other tokenizers use other conventions (a leading-space marker, or a continuation marker such as ##), but the goal is the same: be able to reconstruct the text exactly.

title: Tokenization and Byte-Pair Encoding: How LLMs Turn Text into Numbers
text:
3. When characters themselves are unknown
Try mug with our merges. The letter m was never in the corpus, so it is not in the base vocabulary, and the tokenizer can only emit <unk> for it. The original paper notes this limitation: the only symbols unknown at test time are unseen characters, or symbols whose every occurrence in the training text was merged into larger ones. The second case is rarer. A symbol can stay in the merge list but vanish from the segmented training text. Our toy shows the same thing. After five merges the segmented corpus is hug ×10, pug ×5, pun ×12, b un ×4, hug s ×5. The symbol ug is still in the merge list (it was merge 1), so it counts towards the vocabulary size. But in the segmented text it never stands alone: every ug now sits inside hug or pug. A network trained on this text gets no training examples for ug by itself. Yet a new word like bug is split by replaying the merges into b + ug, which hands the network a symbol it has never seen on its own. In practice the paper left such infrequent subword units out of the network’s vocabulary, so such a symbol is simply unknown to the model. The paper’s own example is safeguar, which only ever occurred inside safeguard. The authors saw no such cases at test time, and note they could be fixed by undoing specific merges.
Unicode contains well over a hundred thousand characters, so a base vocabulary of “every character” is large and still incomplete. Byte-level BPE fixes this by starting from bytes instead of characters. Every string, in any script, is a sequence of UTF-8 bytes, so a base vocabulary of just 256 entries can encode anything and unknown tokens become impossible. GPT-2 popularised this: its vocabulary of 50,257 entries is 256 byte tokens, 50,000 learned merges and one special end-of-text token.
The cost is that non-Latin text starts out longer. In UTF-8, é takes 2 bytes, an emoji 4 bytes, and the Hindi word नमस्ते (6 characters) takes 18 bytes. Until merges cover those byte patterns, such text costs many more tokens than English. We come back to this below.
A related fix is byte fallback in SentencePiece-style tokenizers: keep a normal character vocabulary, and decompose rare characters into byte tokens only when needed.

title: Tokenization and Byte-Pair Encoding: How LLMs Turn Text into Numbers
text:
4. The cousins: WordPiece and Unigram
BPE is not the only way to choose a subword vocabulary. Two others are also worth knowing atleast at the intuition level.
WordPiece (Schuster & Nakajima, 2012; used by BERT, Devlin et al., 2019) also grows its vocabulary bottom-up, but chooses merges by their effect on the likelihood of the training data, not by raw count. The original criterion is the total likelihood gain. The version taught in most tutorials is a simplification that ranks pairs by the gain per occurrence (see the complete mathematical derivation here).
In practice, that reduces to ranking candidate pairs \((a, b)\) by
\[\text{score}(a,b) = \frac{\text{count}(ab)}{\text{count}(a)\,\cdot\,\text{count}(b)}\]
where \(\text{count}(ab)\) is how often \(a\) and \(b\) occur side by side as a pair, and \(\text{count}(a)\), \(\text{count}(b)\) are how often each piece occurs anywhere in the corpus.
Why the denominator matters. Notice that we can rewrite the score as \(\frac{\text{count}(ab)}{\text{count}(a)} \cdot \frac{1}{\text{count}(b)}\), where \(\frac{\text{count}(ab)}{\text{count}(a)}\) is basically \(P(b \text{ follows } a \mid a \text{ just appeared})\). Let’s consider a pair of very common letters like e and s and let’s say, \(\text{count}(es) = 1{,}000\), \(\text{count}(e) = 20{,}000\) and \(\text{count}(s) = 15{,}000\). That means only \(5\%\) of e’s are actually followed by s, and the huge denominator (\(20{,}000 \times 15{,}000\)) pushes the score down to \(3.3 \times 10^{-6}\). Conversely, q and u might only appear together \(150\) times, but almost every q is followed by u (\(\text{count}(q) = 150\), \(\text{count}(u) = 3{,}000\)), giving a score of \(3.3 \times 10^{-4}\), which is a hundred times higher despite being seven times rarer. While BPE merges the most frequent neighbours first, WordPiece merges the most mutually predictive (“sticky”) neighbours first.
At encoding time, rather than replaying a merge list, WordPiece splits each word greedily by matching the longest known vocabulary entry from left to right.
Unigram LM (Kudo, 2018) works top-down. Start with a very large candidate vocabulary and prune. It assumes each subword occurs independently, so a segmentation \(\mathbf{x} = (x_1, \dots, x_M)\) of a sentence has probability
\[P(\mathbf{x}) = \prod_{i=1}^{M} p(x_i)\]
where \(M\) is the number of pieces and \(p(x_i)\) is the probability of piece \(x_i\). The best segmentation is the one with the highest \(P(\mathbf{x})\). Training repeatedly estimates the probabilities \(p(\cdot)\), measures how much the total likelihood would drop if each piece were removed, and discards the least useful ones. A side effect is that Unigram can output several plausible segmentations with probabilities, which Kudo used as a regulariser during training.
SentencePiece (Kudo & Richardson, 2018) is a library, not an algorithm: it can train either BPE or Unigram models, and it treats whitespace as an ordinary symbol so it needs no language-specific pre-splitting.

title: Tokenization and Byte-Pair Encoding: How LLMs Turn Text into Numbers
text:
5. Practical consequences
Vocabulary size is a trade-off, not a constant. A larger vocabulary shortens sequences (cheaper, more text fits in context because it possesses specific tokens for many whole words) but makes the embedding table and output layer bigger and gives rare tokens fewer training examples. Real systems range from about 30K (BERT) to 128K (Llama 3) and beyond. Sennrich et al. themselves describe their choice of vocabulary size as “somewhat arbitrary”.
Fertility. The fertility of a tokenizer on a text is the average number of tokens per word:
\[f = \frac{\text{number of tokens}}{\text{number of words}}\]
The minimum is \(f = 1\), meaning every word is a single token. Higher is worse: more tokens means a higher bill, less room in the context window and more latency. Rust et al. (2021) show fertility rising sharply for languages that are poorly covered by a tokenizer’s vocabulary. The Llama 3 report quotes an average compression gain on English from 3.17 to 3.94 characters per token versus Llama 2, which is the same idea measured the other way around.
Numbers. A plain BPE vocabulary can split numbers inconsistently (“2024” might be one token while “2025” is two), which hurts arithmetic because digits no longer line up by place value. Tokenizers address this differently. Per a Hugging Face write-up on the topic, Llama 1/2 split every number into single digits, while Llama 3 groups digits in chunks of up to three. There is no single right answer; the point is that the choice is made in the tokenizer, before the model ever trains.
Code. Indentation and repeated whitespace can burn many tokens unless the vocabulary contains merged whitespace pieces. Code-heavy training data usually leads to those being learned.

title: Tokenization and Byte-Pair Encoding: How LLMs Turn Text into Numbers
text:
6. Special tokens and chat templates
Some vocabulary entries are not learned from text. Special tokens are reserved symbols that carry structure, not language. They must stay atomic: the tokenizer must never split them into characters.







Token (typical role)
Purpose




Beginning-of-sequence (BOS)
Marks where a sequence starts


End-of-sequence (EOS)
The model emits it to say “I’m done”; generation stops when it appears


Padding (PAD)
Fills shorter sequences in a batch to equal length; masked out of attention


Role markers
Mark who is speaking (system, user, assistant) in chat models



Not every tokenizer has all of them. GPT-2, for instance, has exactly one special token, end-of-text.
Chat models are trained on conversations flattened into one token stream with role markers. A purely illustrative example (real markers differ between model families):
<|system|> You are a helpful assistant. <|end|>
<|user|> Explain BPE in one sentence. <|end|>
<|assistant|>
The model then continues from <|assistant|> until it emits its end-of-turn token. Because every family uses different markers, never hand-build these strings. Use the tokenizer’s own chat template (shown below). It is also why EOS matters so much: a model that cannot emit its stop token keeps generating until a length limit cuts it off.

title: Tokenization and Byte-Pair Encoding: How LLMs Turn Text into Numbers
text:
7. Code

BPE from scratch
from collections import Counter

def get_pair_counts(corpus):
    """corpus: {tuple_of_symbols: count} -> Counter of adjacent pairs."""
    pairs = Counter()
    for symbols, freq in corpus.items():
        for a, b in zip(symbols, symbols[1:]):
            pairs[(a, b)] += freq
    return pairs

def apply_merge(corpus, pair):
    """Replace every adjacent occurrence of `pair` with the merged symbol."""
    merged = pair[0] + pair[1]
    new_corpus = {}
    for symbols, freq in corpus.items():
        out, i = [], 0
        while i < len(symbols):
            if i < len(symbols) - 1 and (symbols[i], symbols[i + 1]) == pair:
                out.append(merged); i += 2
            else:
                out.append(symbols[i]); i += 1
        key = tuple(out)
        new_corpus[key] = new_corpus.get(key, 0) + freq
    return new_corpus

def train_bpe(word_counts, num_merges):
    corpus = {tuple(w): c for w, c in word_counts.items()}
    base_vocab = sorted({ch for w in word_counts for ch in w})
    merges = []
    for _ in range(num_merges):
        pairs = get_pair_counts(corpus)
        if not pairs:
            break
        best, count = pairs.most_common(1)[0]   # ties: first pair seen wins
        corpus = apply_merge(corpus, best)
        merges.append((best, count))
    return base_vocab, merges

def encode(word, merges, base_vocab):
    """Split into characters, then replay the merges in learned order."""
    symbols = tuple(word)
    for pair, _ in merges:
        symbols = next(iter(apply_merge({symbols: 1}, pair)))
    return [s if (len(s) > 1 or s in base_vocab) else "<unk>" for s in symbols]

counts = {"hug": 10, "pug": 5, "pun": 12, "bun": 4, "hugs": 5}
base, merges = train_bpe(counts, 3)
for pair, c in merges:
    print(pair, c)
print(encode("bugs", merges, base))   # ['b', 'ug', 's']
print(encode("mug", merges, base))    # ['<unk>', 'ug']
Output:
('u', 'g') 20
('u', 'n') 16
('h', 'ug') 15
['b', 'ug', 's']
['<unk>', 'ug']
Real implementations add the pieces we skipped: an end-of-word or leading-space convention, byte-level base symbols, and incremental pair-count updates instead of recounting the corpus on every merge.


A real tokenizer with Hugging Face transformers
from transformers import AutoTokenizer

tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("gpt2")        # byte-level BPE, 50,257 entries

text = "Tokenization is unbelievably useful."
ids = tok.encode(text)
print(ids)                                          # integer IDs
print(tok.convert_ids_to_tokens(ids))               # the subword pieces
assert tok.decode(ids) == text                      # lossless round trip

# Chat models ship their own template; use it instead of hand-built strings.
chat_tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("<a-chat-model-name>")
messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "Explain BPE in one sentence."}]
prompt = chat_tok.apply_chat_template(
    messages, tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True
)
print(prompt)                                       # shows the model's real markers
Run it with a few of your own sentences, including another language and some code, and compare token counts. Seeing the pieces is the fastest way to build intuition.

title: Tokenization and Byte-Pair Encoding: How LLMs Turn Text into Numbers
text:
8. Common pitfalls

Tokens are not words. English averages a bit over one token per word, but the ratio varies a lot by language and domain. Estimate cost and context use in tokens, never in words.
The tokenizer belongs to the model. IDs only mean something to the vocabulary and embedding table they were trained with. Swapping tokenizers without retraining breaks the model silently.
Whitespace is part of the token. In many tokenizers hello and hello (with a leading space) are different tokens. A stray trailing space in a prompt can change what the model sees.
Unknown characters. A character-level base vocabulary can emit <unk> and lose information. Byte-level BPE avoids this, at the cost of longer sequences for scripts that UTF-8 encodes in several bytes.
Inconsistent number splitting. Do not assume digits are tokenized the same way across models or even across similar numbers. Check before trusting a model on arithmetic or on parsing numeric IDs.
Reading a high fertility as “the model is bad at this language”. It is a symptom of tokenizer coverage, and it directly raises cost and shrinks effective context. Measure it on your own text.
Hand-writing chat templates. A single wrong role marker or missing end-of-turn token can degrade output with no error. Use the template that ships with the tokenizer.
Letting user text become control tokens. If user-supplied text containing a special-token string is parsed as the real special token, it can corrupt the prompt structure. Treat user text as plain text.
Adding new special tokens and expecting them to work. Tokens added after pretraining get embeddings that are untrained until fine-tuning teaches the model what they mean.
Mismatched tokenization between training stages. Anything that compares two models’ token probabilities (as RL fine-tuning methods do) requires both to use identical tokenization and special-token handling.

title: Tokenization and Byte-Pair Encoding: How LLMs Turn Text into Numbers
text:
Takeaways

Models read integers; the tokenizer is the translation layer and it is learned from data.
Subwords give a middle path: short sequences and an open vocabulary.
BPE learns an ordered list of merges. Learn by repeatedly merging the most frequent pair (recounting each time), encode by replaying the merges in order.
Vocabulary size = base symbols + merges.
Byte-level BPE guarantees no unknown tokens; special tokens add structure; and tokenizer choices, from vocabulary size to digit handling, directly affect cost and capability.
