title: Companion: Deriving the Whitening Matrix
text: This page is a companion to Anisotropy and Whitening. It derives the whitening matrix and a few facts the main article uses. It assumes basic linear algebra (matrix product, transpose, eigendecomposition).

title: Companion: Deriving the Whitening Matrix
text:
Setup
We have \(N\) embeddings, stored as row vectors \(\mathbf{x}_i \in \mathbb{R}^{1\times d}\). Define
\[
\boldsymbol{\mu} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbf{x}_i, \qquad
\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol{\mu})^\top(\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol{\mu}) \in \mathbb{R}^{d\times d}.
\]
\(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) is symmetric and positive semi-definite; we assume it is positive definite (all eigenvalues \(>0\), which needs enough data and no perfectly redundant coordinates).
We look for a \(d\times d\) matrix \(\mathbf{W}\) such that \(\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_i = (\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol{\mu})\,\mathbf{W}\) has mean \(\mathbf{0}\) and covariance \(\mathbf{I}\).

title: Companion: Deriving the Whitening Matrix
section: Step 1: mean and covariance of the transformed data
text:
Step 1: mean and covariance of the transformed data
Mean. \(\frac1N\sum_i \tilde{\mathbf{x}}_i = \left(\frac1N\sum_i \mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}\right)\mathbf{W} = \mathbf{0}\). Subtracting \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) already makes it zero for any \(\mathbf{W}\).
Covariance. Since the mean is zero,
\[
\tilde{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}
= \frac1N\sum_i \tilde{\mathbf{x}}_i^\top\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_i
= \frac1N\sum_i \mathbf{W}^\top(\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol{\mu})^\top(\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol{\mu})\mathbf{W}
= \mathbf{W}^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\,\mathbf{W}.
\]
So the requirement is the single matrix equation
\[
\mathbf{W}^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\,\mathbf{W} = \mathbf{I}. \tag{1}
\]

title: Companion: Deriving the Whitening Matrix
text:
Step 2: diagonalise \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\)
A symmetric positive definite matrix has an eigendecomposition (the spectral theorem; for such matrices it coincides with the SVD):
\[
\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{U}^\top,
\]
where \(\mathbf{U}\) is orthogonal (\(\mathbf{U}^\top\mathbf{U}=\mathbf{I}\)) and \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}=\text{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_d)\) with \(\lambda_1\ge\dots\ge\lambda_d>0\).

title: Companion: Deriving the Whitening Matrix
text:
Step 3: solve for \(\mathbf{W}\)
Try \(\mathbf{W} = \mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1/2}\), where \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1/2}=\text{diag}(\lambda_1^{-1/2},\dots,\lambda_d^{-1/2})\). Then
\[
\mathbf{W}^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{W}
= \boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1/2}\mathbf{U}^\top(\mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{U}^\top)\mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1/2}
= \boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1/2}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1/2}
= \mathbf{I}.
\]
It uses \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1/2}\) being diagonal (so equal to its own transpose) and \(\mathbf{U}^\top\mathbf{U}=\mathbf{I}\). This matches the solution in Su et al. (2021), who reach it by writing \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=(\mathbf{W}^{-1})^\top\mathbf{W}^{-1}\) and choosing \(\mathbf{W}^{-1}=\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{1/2}\mathbf{U}^\top\).
In column-vector notation, a vector \(\mathbf{h}\) is whitened as \(\tilde{\mathbf{h}}=\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1/2}\mathbf{U}^\top(\mathbf{h}-\boldsymbol{\mu})\), which is the transpose of \((\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})\mathbf{W}\).

The solution is not unique
If \(\mathbf{R}\) is any orthogonal matrix, then \(\mathbf{W}'=\mathbf{W}\mathbf{R}\) also satisfies equation (1), since \(\mathbf{R}^\top\mathbf{I}\mathbf{R}=\mathbf{I}\). Different choices of \(\mathbf{R}\) give different “whitenings” with the same covariance. Choosing \(\mathbf{R}=\mathbf{I}\) gives \(\mathbf{W}=\mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1/2}\) (often called PCA whitening); choosing \(\mathbf{R}=\mathbf{U}^\top\) gives \(\mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1/2}\mathbf{U}^\top\) (ZCA whitening), which stays as close as possible to the original coordinates. Because a rotation does not change any cosine similarity between whitened vectors, both choices give the same pairwise cosines.

title: Companion: Deriving the Whitening Matrix
text:
Step 4: dropping directions (Whitening-\(k\))
Let \(\mathbf{W}_k=\mathbf{W}[:,:k]\) be the first \(k\) columns, i.e. \(\mathbf{U}_k\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_k^{-1/2}\). The transformed vectors \(\tilde{\mathbf{x}}^{(k)}_i=(\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol{\mu})\mathbf{W}_k\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times k}\) have covariance
\[
\mathbf{W}_k^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{W}_k = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_k^{-1/2}\mathbf{U}_k^\top\mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{U}^\top\mathbf{U}_k\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_k^{-1/2} = \mathbf{I}_k,
\]
because \(\mathbf{U}_k^\top\mathbf{U}=[\,\mathbf{I}_k\;\;\mathbf{0}\,]\). So the retained coordinates are still uncorrelated with unit variance. The discarded directions are the ones with the smallest variances \(\lambda_{k+1},\dots,\lambda_d\). Projecting onto the top-\(k\) eigenvectors is exactly PCA, and Whitening-\(k\) is PCA plus rescaling each kept axis by \(1/\sqrt{\lambda_j}\).

title: Companion: Deriving the Whitening Matrix
text:
Streaming the mean and covariance
For large corpora we want \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) and \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) without holding all vectors in memory. Let \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_n,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_n\) be the statistics of the first \(n\) vectors (covariance taken about the running mean, as above). Adding \(\mathbf{x}_{n+1}\):
\[
\boldsymbol{\mu}_{n+1} = \frac{n}{n+1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_n + \frac{1}{n+1}\mathbf{x}_{n+1}.
\]
For the covariance, write \(\mathbf{S}_n = n\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_n\). The standard (Welford-style) update is
\[
\mathbf{S}_{n+1} = \mathbf{S}_n + (\mathbf{x}_{n+1}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_n)^\top(\mathbf{x}_{n+1}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{n+1}),
\]
and since \(\mathbf{x}_{n+1}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{n+1}=\frac{n}{n+1}(\mathbf{x}_{n+1}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_n)\), dividing by \(n+1\) gives the exact recursion
\[
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{n+1} = \frac{n}{n+1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_n + \frac{n}{(n+1)^2}(\mathbf{x}_{n+1}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_n)^\top(\mathbf{x}_{n+1}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_n).
\]
Memory is \(O(d^2)\) regardless of \(N\), and time is \(O(d^2)\) per vector.

title: Companion: Deriving the Whitening Matrix
text:
Why this matters for cosine
After whitening, \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) no longer contributes a shared offset to dot products, and each (kept) direction contributes equally to \(\mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{y}\). That is the “isotropic, so the coordinate formula for cosine is trustworthy” argument of the main article, and also the reason full whitening can hurt: directions with tiny variance, often mostly noise, are given the same weight as the informative ones (see the Spectral Noise Amplification section below).

title: Companion: Deriving the Whitening Matrix
section: Numerical Stability, Rank Deficiency, and Regularization
text:
Numerical Stability, Rank Deficiency, and Regularization
While \(\mathbf{W} = \mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1/2}\) is exact in theory, applying it blindly at full rank (\(k = d\)) introduces two practical failure modes: noise amplification in ill-conditioned directions and singularity when the sample size \(N\) is small.

1. Spectral Noise Amplification
Writing \(\mathbf{U} = [\mathbf{u}_1, \mathbf{u}_2, \dots, \mathbf{u}_d]\) in terms of its column eigenvectors shows how \(\mathbf{W}\) acts on each principal axis independently:
\[
\mathbf{W} = \mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1/2} = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{\mathbf{u}_1}{\sqrt{\lambda_1}} & \dfrac{\mathbf{u}_2}{\sqrt{\lambda_2}} & \cdots & \dfrac{\mathbf{u}_d}{\sqrt{\lambda_d}} \end{bmatrix}
\]
For a centered embedding \(\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}\), its \(j\)-th whitened coordinate is:
\[
\tilde{x}_{i,j} = \frac{(\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu})\,\mathbf{u}_j}{\sqrt{\lambda_j}}
\]
In anisotropic transformer embedding spaces, the eigenvalue spectrum decays rapidly. The leading eigenvalues capture dominant semantic and structural variance, whereas the tail eigenvalues (\(\lambda_j \to 0\)) often reflect floating-point roundoff or quantization noise. If \(\lambda_d = 10^{-8}\), dividing by \(\sqrt{\lambda_d}\) multiplies projections along \(\mathbf{u}_d\) by \(10^4\). Full-rank whitening forces every axis to unit variance (\(\lambda = 1\)), giving a pure-noise tail direction the exact same weight in downstream cosine similarity as the top principal component.


2. Rank Deficiency When \(N \le d\)
Let \(\mathbf{X}_c \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d}\) denote the mean-centered embedding matrix with rows \(\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}\), so that \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \frac{1}{N}\mathbf{X}_c^\top \mathbf{X}_c\). Because the rows of \(\mathbf{X}_c\) sum to the zero vector, \(\sum_{i=1}^{N}(\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}) = \mathbf{0}\), they are linearly dependent and span a subspace of dimension at most \(N - 1\). Consequently:
\[
\operatorname{rank}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}) = \operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{X}_c^\top \mathbf{X}_c) = \operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{X}_c) \le \min(N - 1, d)
\]
Whenever \(N \le d\), \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) is rank-deficient (singular). At least \(d - N + 1\) eigenvalues are identically zero (\(\lambda_j = 0\), or \(\approx 10^{-16}\) in finite precision), making \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1/2}\) undefined due to division by zero.


3. Two Remedies: Truncation vs. Tikhonov Regularization
To guarantee a well-conditioned transformation, we can either truncate the spectrum or regularize the diagonal:

Spectral Truncation (Whitening-\(k\)): Keep only the top \(k \le \operatorname{rank}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})\) columns of \(\mathbf{W}\) corresponding to signal-bearing eigenvalues, discarding the noisy or zero-variance tail: \[
\mathbf{W}_k = \mathbf{U}_{:, :k}\,\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{:k, :k}^{-1/2} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k}
\]
Tikhonov Regularization (Diagonal Loading): Add a small damping constant \(\epsilon > 0\) (typically \(10^{-5}\) to \(10^{-8}\)) to the covariance diagonal before inversion, \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\text{reg}} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma} + \epsilon\mathbf{I}\), which shifts all eigenvalues by \(+\epsilon\): \[
\mathbf{W}_{\text{reg}} = \mathbf{U}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda} + \epsilon\mathbf{I})^{-1/2}, \qquad \text{scaling axis } j \text{ by } \frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda_j + \epsilon}}
\] This bounds the maximum amplification factor at \(1/\sqrt{\epsilon}\) and prevents division by zero even when \(\lambda_j = 0\).

title: Positional Encoding Basics: Why Transformers Need Positions
text: Take the sentence “the cat sat on the mat” and shuffle it into “mat the on sat cat the”. A transformer layer (without a causal mask), as originally defined, produces the same vector for the token “sat” in both cases. Self-attention has no built-in notion of order. This article covers why, what we do about it, and four classic answers: sinusoidal, learned absolute, relative biases, and ALiBi. Part 9 covers rotary embeddings (RoPE), and Part 10 covers stretching a model to longer contexts.

title: Positional Encoding Basics: Why Transformers Need Positions
section: 1. The problem: attention is a set operation
text:
1. The problem: attention is a set operation
For a sequence of token vectors \(x_1,\dots,x_N \in \mathbb{R}^d\) (rows of a matrix \(X\)), one attention head computes
\[
\text{Attn}(X) = \text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{(XW_q)(XW_k)^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) XW_v
\]
Symbols:

\(W_q, W_k, W_v\) are learned projection matrices; \(q_i = W_q^\top x_i\), \(k_j = W_k^\top x_j\), \(v_j = W_v^\top x_j\) are the query, key and value of token \(i\) or \(j\).
\(d_k\) is the key dimension; dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) keeps the scores at a stable scale.
The score between tokens \(i\) and \(j\) is \(q_i^\top k_j / \sqrt{d_k}\). It depends only on the contents of \(x_i\) and \(x_j\).

Now permute the rows of \(X\) with a permutation matrix \(P\). Every score is the same pair of contents, just moved to a new row and column, so the output is permuted the same way: \(\text{Attn}(PX) = P\,\text{Attn}(X)\). This property is called permutation equivariance. Each token’s output vector is identical whatever order the other tokens arrive in. The feed-forward layers act on each token separately, so they don’t add order information either.
To a pure attention stack, a sentence is a bag of tokens. Word order obviously matters (“dog bites man” is not “man bites dog”), so we have to inject it.

A subtlety: causal masks leak a little position
Decoder-only language models use a causal mask: token \(i\) may only attend to tokens \(j \le i\). This breaks the symmetry slightly. Token \(i\) averages over exactly \(i\) tokens, so in principle a model can infer “how many tokens came before me” and so approximate its absolute position. Haviv et al. (2022) trained causal language models with no positional encoding at all and found they stay competitive, and probing showed they learn an implicit notion of absolute position. The same trick does not work for bidirectional (masked) language models, which failed to converge without position information.
So the causal mask provides a weak, absolute, implicit signal. Explicit positional encodings give a stronger and cleaner one, and they are what the rest of this series is about.

title: Positional Encoding Basics: Why Transformers Need Positions
text:
2. Where can position enter?
There are three natural places, and each classic method picks one.





flowchart LR
  A["<b>Token embedding</b><br/>xᵢ ∈ ℝᵈ"] -->|"① add position<br/>xᵢ + pᵢ"| B["<b>Projections</b><br/>qᵢ = W_q xᵢ, kⱼ = W_k xⱼ"]
  B -->|"③ rotate q, k<br/>(RoPE, Part 9)"| C["<b>Scores</b><br/>sᵢⱼ = qᵢᵀ kⱼ / √d_k"]
  C -->|"② subtract distance penalty<br/>sᵢⱼ − m·(i−j)"| D["<b>Softmax and weighted sum</b><br/>Σⱼ aᵢⱼ vⱼ"]







Add to the input (sinusoidal, learned absolute): the position vector \(p_i\) is added directly to the token embedding before the first layer.
Bias the scores (relative-position biases, ALiBi): leave the vectors alone and add a distance-dependent number to each attention score.
Rotate queries and keys (RoPE): transform \(q\) and \(k\) by a position-dependent rotation. This is Part 9.

Good positional information should do four things:

distinguish different orders;
make relative distance easy to use (a phrase means the same thing at position 5 or position 5000);
keep working on sequences longer than anything seen in training;
cost little compute and few parameters.

The methods below trade these off differently.

title: Positional Encoding Basics: Why Transformers Need Positions
text:
3. Sinusoidal encoding (original Transformer)

3.1 Start with a binary counter
How would you tag positions \(0,1,2,\dots\) with numbers a network can use? The raw integer \(pos\) is a poor choice: it is unbounded, and large values would swamp the token embedding. Binary counting suggests something better. Here are the first eight positions written with three bits:

Read down each column:


the rightmost bit (bit 0, the least significant) flips at every step;
the middle bit flips every 2 steps;
the leftmost bit flips every 4 steps.

Each bit flips at half the rate of the bit to its right. Together the bits give every position a unique code, and \(n\) bits are enough for \(2^n\) positions. Notice the division of labour: the fast bits tell neighbours apart (position 6 versus 7), while the slow bits say roughly where you are (first half versus second half). A cascade of frequencies gives both fine and coarse position information from a handful of numbers.
Bits are a poor fit for a neural network, though. Each bit is a square wave that jumps between exactly 0 and 1. That is discrete and not differentiable.


3.2 From bits to sinusoids
Vaswani et al. (2017) kept the idea of cascading frequencies, not the square wave. They did not use sinusoids as a smooth squiggle that approximates the exact 0s and 1s of a bit. They wanted a continuous version of the counter, where each embedding dimension plays the role of one bit:

the lowest dimensions act like the rightmost bits and oscillate rapidly;
the highest dimensions act like the leftmost bits and turn incredibly slowly;
instead of flipping between 0 and 1, each dimension moves smoothly in \([-1, 1]\), so it is bounded and differentiable, and nearby positions get nearby vectors.

Reading the values of all the waves at once gives a fingerprint of the position.
Concretely, the encoding adds a fixed vector \(PE(pos) \in \mathbb{R}^d\) to the embedding of the token at position \(pos\):
\[
PE(pos, 2i) = \sin\!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d}}\right), \qquad
PE(pos, 2i+1) = \cos\!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d}}\right)
\]
Symbols: \(pos = 0,1,2,\dots\) is the token position; \(d\) is the model dimension; \(i = 0,\dots,d/2-1\) indexes a pair of dimensions (a sine and a cosine of the same frequency), so dimension \(2i\) is a sine and \(2i+1\) a cosine.
Intuition. Think of a clock with many hands. Pair \(i\) is one hand that completes a full turn every \(\lambda_i = 2\pi \cdot 10000^{2i/d}\) positions. The first pair turns every \(2\pi \approx 6\) tokens. The slowest turns roughly every \(2\pi \cdot 10000 \approx 63{,}000\) tokens. Together the hands give each position a unique fingerprint, like the digits of a counter where low digits flip fast and high digits flip slowly. The geometric spacing of wavelengths covers many scales with few dimensions.
The binary analogy has limits: bit periods double each time (2, 4, 8, …), while here the wavelengths grow by the constant factor \(10000^{2/d}\) from one pair to the next, so they span a much wider range with the same number of dimensions.


3.3 What the encoding looks like



The sinusoidal encoding for \(d=128\) and positions 0 to 49. Each row is the positional vector of one position; each column is one embedding dimension. Colour is the value in \([-1, 1]\).


Read the picture as a stack of position vectors: row \(pos\) is \(PE(pos)\), and the columns are the dimensions \(0,\dots,127\).

Left side (low dimensions, like the rightmost bits): the colours change quickly as you move down through the positions. These are the fast waves, and they separate neighbouring positions.
Right side (high dimensions, like the leftmost bits): the colour barely changes down the column. These are the slow waves; over these 50 positions they are almost constant. The thin vertical stripes there come from the even and odd dimensions alternating between a sine (close to 0) and a cosine (close to 1) of the same slow frequency.
The curved bands are explained below.

How to read it. Draw a horizontal line at any position \(pos\). The sequence of colours (values) along that line, across all the different frequencies, is the positional vector for a token at position \(pos\). Move one row down and the left part changes a lot while the right part hardly moves. Two different positions would have to agree on every column at once to get the same vector, and with wavelengths that don’t line up with each other that does not happen in practice within the range of lengths we use.

Why the bands curve
The curved bands are contours of constant phase. For an even (sine) column \(x\), the value at row \(pos\) is \(\sin\theta\), where the phase is
\[
\theta(pos, x) = \frac{pos}{10000^{x/d}}, \qquad d = 128
\]
A band of one colour follows the cells where \(\theta\) equals a fixed value \(C\): for example \(C=\pi/2\) for the first dark-blue peak, \(C=\pi\) for the first zero crossing, and \(C=3\pi/2\) for the first dark-red trough. Solving \(\theta = C\) for the row gives the shape of the band:
\[
pos(x) = C \cdot 10000^{x/d}
\]
Because \(x\) sits in the exponent, every band is an exponential curve. The intuition: moving right, the frequency drops exponentially, so you must go further down the sequence (larger \(pos\)) before the wave reaches the same phase. Tracing the “first peak” across slower and slower columns draws a curve that dives from the top left towards the bottom right (position 0 is at the top of the plot).
Where does each band meet the bottom edge, the last row \(pos=49\)?
\[
pos(x) = C \cdot 10000^{x/d} \implies x = \frac{d}{4}\,\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{pos}{C}\right) = 32\,\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{49}{C}\right)
\]

Around column 38 it has gone up and come back to zero. Around column 33 it has reached the bottom of its first trough. To the left of that, more cycles stack up, tighter and steeper, until they look like noise.
One more detail: each cosine column (odd \(x\)) has the same frequency as the sine column to its left but is shifted by a quarter wavelength, so the plot is two interleaved patterns. For example, to the right of column ≈ 48 both sine and cosine values are positive at the bottom row, which gives the broad blue region there.



3.4 Why sine and cosine?
The authors chose this specific mathematical pairing to satisfy a hypothesis: the model could learn to attend by relative position if any positional shift \(PE(pos+k)\) could be represented as a simple linear function of \(PE(pos)\). The sine and cosine pair achieves exactly this. For one pair with angular frequency \(\omega_i = 10000^{-2i/d}\):
\[
\begin{pmatrix}\sin\omega_i(pos+k)\\ \cos\omega_i(pos+k)\end{pmatrix}
=
\underbrace{\begin{pmatrix}\cos\omega_i k & \sin\omega_i k\\ -\sin\omega_i k & \cos\omega_i k\end{pmatrix}}_{\text{rotation by } \omega_i k,\ \text{depends only on } k}
\begin{pmatrix}\sin\omega_i pos\\ \cos\omega_i pos\end{pmatrix}
\]
Shifting a position by \(k\) rotates each pair by an angle that depends only on \(k\). Keep this “shift = rotation” picture in mind: RoPE in Part 9 is built on exactly this idea, applied in a different place.


3.5 Trade-offs
No parameters, deterministic, and defined for any position. But it is added once at the input, so position has to survive through all layers, and the model must learn to decode relative offsets from absolute fingerprints. In practice the extrapolation is poor: Press et al. (2022) showed that a sinusoidal model, although it technically can be evaluated at longer lengths, extrapolates very little beyond its training length. Because the network has never encountered those higher positions during training, it simply hasn’t learned how to interpret their novel positional signals. The original paper also tried learned position embeddings and found nearly identical results.

title: Positional Encoding Basics: Why Transformers Need Positions
text:
4. Learned absolute embeddings
GPT-2 and BERT instead keep a trainable table \(E_{pos} \in \mathbb{R}^{L_{max}\times d}\) and compute the input as
\[
h_0^{(pos)} = \text{TokenEmbed}(x_{pos}) + E_{pos}[pos]
\]
Symbols: \(L_{max}\) is the maximum supported length (for example 512 for BERT, 1024 for GPT-2); row \(pos\) of the table is the learned vector for that position.

Pros: maximum flexibility, simple to implement, works well within the training length.
Cons: it adds \(L_{max}\times d\) parameters (for example \(2048 \times 768 \approx 1.6\)M). There is no row at all for positions beyond \(L_{max}\), so the model cannot be used past it without new training. Rows for rarely used late positions also see little training signal and stay under-trained.

title: Positional Encoding Basics: Why Transformers Need Positions
text:
5. Relative position biases
Language mostly cares about how far apart tokens are, not their absolute index. Several methods make that explicit by feeding the relative distance \(i - j\) into attention:

Shaw et al. (2018) add learned relative-position embeddings (indexed by the distance, clipped to a maximum) to the keys and values. The clipping encodes the hypothesis that precise distance stops mattering beyond some range.
T5 (Raffel et al., 2020) adds a learned scalar bias \(b_{i,j}\) to each attention score, shared among bucketed distances.

Written as the attention score \(s_{ij}\) between a query at position \(i\) and a key at position \(j\) (with \(r = i-j\) the relative distance), the two ideas are:
\[
\underbrace{s_{ij} = \frac{q_i^\top\big(k_j + a_{\mathrm{clip}(r,\,-c,\,c)}\big)}{\sqrt{d_k}}}_{\text{Shaw et al.}}
\qquad\qquad
\underbrace{s_{ij} = q_i^\top k_j + b_{\mathrm{bucket}(r)}}_{\text{T5}}
\]
Symbols: \(a_{\rho}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_k}\) is a learned vector for each clipped distance \(\rho\in\{-c,\dots,c\}\) (so distances beyond \(c\) share one vector), and \(\mathrm{clip}(r,-c,c)=\max(-c,\min(c,r))\). \(b_{\cdot}\in\mathbb{R}\) is a learned scalar for each distance bucket (separate for each head, with buckets that grow wider with distance), and \(\mathrm{bucket}(r)\) maps a distance to its bucket. Shaw et al. also add a second learned vector to the values, \(v_j + a'_{\mathrm{clip}(r,-c,c)}\), which is omitted above. In both cases the usual softmax over \(j\) follows.
Both work inside attention rather than on the input embeddings, so the token vectors stay free of position. T5’s bias touches only the scores; ALiBi pushes that idea to the extreme.

title: Positional Encoding Basics: Why Transformers Need Positions
section: 6. ALiBi: a fixed linear penalty on distance
text:
6. ALiBi: a fixed linear penalty on distance
Press et al. (2022) drop positional embeddings altogether. For a query at position \(i\) and a key at position \(j\), they subtract a penalty proportional to their absolute distance from the attention score:
\[
\text{score}_{ij}^{(h)} = \frac{q_i^\top k_j}{\sqrt{d_k}} - m_h\vert{}i-j\vert{}
\]
When applied to the entire sequence at once, this is equivalent to subtracting a fixed distance matrix (scaled by \(m_h\)) inside the softmax:
\[
\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}} - m \cdot [|i - j|]_{i,j}\right) V
\]
(Note: ALiBi was originally designed for causal language models, where a mask naturally prevents \(j > i\). But using the absolute distance \(\vert{}i-j\vert{}\) makes the penalty mechanism clear for any architecture).
Symbols: \(h\) is the attention head; \(m_h > 0\) is that head’s fixed slope. For \(H\) heads the slopes form a geometric sequence \(m_h = 2^{-8h/H}\) for \(h = 1,\dots,H\); with 8 heads this is \(\tfrac12, \tfrac14, \dots, \tfrac1{256}\). Nothing is learned and nothing is added to the embeddings.
Intuition. The penalty is a built-in recency prior: nearby tokens get a head start, and the farther away a token is, the lower its score. Steep heads (large \(m_h\)) look almost only at the last few tokens. Shallow heads (small \(m_h\)) can still reach far back. So the heads together give multi-scale locality.
Headline result. Normally, if you want a model to handle 2048 tokens, you have to train it on 2048 tokens. The researchers showed that a 1.3B-parameter ALiBi model trained only on short sequences (1024 tokens) matched the performance of a traditional sinusoidal model explicitly trained on long sequences (2048 tokens). Because the ALiBi model could achieve this while training on half the sequence length, it trained 11% faster and used 11% less memory.
Caveats. The bias is fixed, so the model cannot reshape it. A strong recency prior suits language modeling but may not suit every task. Later work reports that ALiBi’s extrapolation, while better than sinusoidal, is still limited rather than unbounded (for instance, the YaRN paper summarizes it as only “limited generalization”). Most recent open models moved to RoPE instead (Part 2).

title: Positional Encoding Basics: Why Transformers Need Positions
text:
Common pitfalls

Assuming “defined for any position” means “works at any position.” The sinusoidal formula can be evaluated anywhere, but a model trained on short sequences still behaves poorly on long ones.
Scale mismatch when adding position to embeddings. The original Transformer multiplies the token embeddings by \(\sqrt{d}\) before adding \(PE\), so the position signal does not drown out (or get drowned by) the content signal. Forgetting this kind of scaling changes training dynamics.
Index errors with learned tables. Inputs longer than \(L_{max}\) raise an error or, worse, get silently truncated or clamped.
Thinking causal models are order-blind. The causal mask leaks a count-like signal, which is why removing positional encodings degrades causal models gracefully but breaks bidirectional ones.

title: Anisotropy and Whitening: Fixing the Geometry of Embeddings
text:
Embeddings are used through geometry: nearest neighbours, clusters, cosine scores. That only works if the geometry is well behaved. This article explains one specific way it often is not (anisotropy), what the research found about it in popular models, and a simple linear fix (whitening) with its dimensionality-reduction variant.
It builds on From Token IDs to Vectors, which introduced embeddings and cosine similarity. The algebra behind the whitening matrix is in a companion derivation page.

title: Anisotropy and Whitening: Fixing the Geometry of Embeddings
text:
What cosine similarity quietly assumes
Cosine similarity compares directions:
\[
\cos(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{d} x_i y_i}{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{d} x_i^2}\,\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{d} y_i^2}}
\]
where \(x_i, y_i\) are the coordinates of the two vectors and \(d\) is the dimension. The formula is written in terms of coordinates, so it measures a geometric angle only if the coordinate axes are a standard orthonormal basis (perpendicular, unit length). Su et al. (2021) use this as a heuristic motivation: if a set of vectors is isotropic, it is reasonable to treat the axes as a good orthonormal basis and trust the formula; if it is not, transform it first and then take cosines. This is a motivating argument and the paper backs it with experiments.

Why non-orthonormal axes break the formula
Suppose our embedding coordinates \((x_1, x_2)\) and \((y_1, y_2)\) are measured along two basis vectors \(\mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2\) that are neither perpendicular nor unit-length:
\[
\mathbf{x} = x_1 \mathbf{b}_1 + x_2 \mathbf{b}_2, \qquad \mathbf{y} = y_1 \mathbf{b}_1 + y_2 \mathbf{b}_2
\]
Taking the true geometric inner product \(\langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \rangle\) expands into four terms, collected by the Gram matrix \(\mathbf{G}_{ij} = \langle \mathbf{b}_i, \mathbf{b}_j \rangle\):
\[
\langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \rangle = x_1 y_1 \|\mathbf{b}_1\|^2 + x_2 y_2 \|\mathbf{b}_2\|^2 + (x_1 y_2 + x_2 y_1)\langle \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2 \rangle = \mathbf{x}^\top \mathbf{G} \mathbf{y}
\]
The standard cosine formula \(\frac{\sum x_i y_i}{\|\mathbf{x}\|\|\mathbf{y}\|}\) silently assumes \(\|\mathbf{b}_1\| = \|\mathbf{b}_2\| = 1\) and \(\langle \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2 \rangle = 0\) (i.e., \(\mathbf{G} = \mathbf{I}\)). When the embedding space is anisotropic, meaning it is stretched along certain directions (\(\|\mathbf{b}_i\| \neq 1\)) or correlated across dimensions (\(\langle \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2 \rangle \neq 0\)), the naive coordinate sum drops the cross-terms and misweights the axes.
This is why Su et al. (2021) apply a whitening transformation \(\tilde{\mathbf{x}} = (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})\mathbf{W}\) before computing cosine similarity: whitening forces the empirical covariance to the identity matrix, effectively rotating and rescaling the coordinate axes back into an orthonormal basis where \(\mathbf{G} = \mathbf{I}\).

title: Anisotropy and Whitening: Fixing the Geometry of Embeddings
text:
Isotropic vs anisotropic
A set of vectors is isotropic if its directions are spread uniformly, with no preferred direction. A practical test (used by Ethayarajh, 2019, following Arora et al., 2017): the average cosine similarity between randomly sampled pairs. For an isotropic set it is about 0. The closer it is to 1, the more anisotropic the set, which geometrically means the vectors sit in a narrow cone.



Isotropic vs anisotropic embedding spaces, and what whitening does.


There are two ingredients that make a cloud of vectors look like that cone:

A shared offset: all vectors have a large common component (a non-zero mean \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\)).
Unequal spread: a few directions have much more variance than the rest. Instead of forming a round sphere, the cloud is stretched into a long cigar (ellipsoid). For example, if the first coordinate typically ranges around \(\pm 100\) while the other \(767\) coordinates range around \(\pm 0.1\), that single high-variance axis dominates \(\sum x_i y_i\), effectively reducing a \(768\)-dimensional comparison to a \(1\)-dimensional check.

Whitening, as we will see, targets both.

title: Anisotropy and Whitening: Fixing the Geometry of Embeddings
text:
What the evidence says: Ethayarajh (2019)
Ethayarajh studied hidden-layer representations (not just the input embedding table) of ELMo (2 layers), BERT-base-cased (12 layers) and GPT-2 (12 layers), plus each model’s input layer as “layer 0”. Input sentences came from the SemEval Semantic Textual Similarity tasks (2012 to 2016), and only words appearing in at least 5 distinct contexts were analysed.






NoteWhy include “layer 0”?



Layer 0 is the raw input layer before any transformer attention or biLSTM mixes information across the sentence. Because layer 0 is not contextualized, it serves as a baseline for comparing how much contextualization each subsequent hidden layer actually adds.



Measuring contextuality
To quantify how “contextual” a representation really is, the paper defines three metrics for a given layer \(\ell\), where \(f_\ell(s, i)\) maps the word at index \(i\) in sentence \(s\) to its vector in layer \(\ell\):
1. Self-similarity (\(\text{SelfSim}\)): Let a word \(w\) appear in \(n\) distinct sentences \(\{s_1, \dots, s_n\}\) at indices \(\{i_1, \dots, i_n\}\). Its self-similarity in layer \(\ell\) is the average pairwise cosine similarity between its representations across those \(n\) contexts:
\[\text{SelfSim}_\ell(w) = \frac{1}{n^2 - n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} \sum_{k \ne j} \cos\big(f_\ell(s_j, i_j),\, f_\ell(s_k, i_k)\big)\]
Intuition: If a layer does not contextualize \(w\) at all, every occurrence gets the exact same vector and \(\text{SelfSim}_\ell(w) = 1\). The more a layer bends \(w\)’s vector to fit its surrounding sentence, the further apart those occurrences drift, and the lower \(\text{SelfSim}_\ell(w)\) drops.
2. Intra-sentence similarity (\(\text{IntraSim}\)): Let \(s = \langle w_1, \dots, w_n \rangle\) be a single sentence of \(n\) words, and let \(\mathbf{s}_\ell = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} f_\ell(s, i)\) be the mean of all word vectors in that sentence. The intra-sentence similarity is the average cosine between each word in \(s\) and the sentence mean:
\[\text{IntraSim}_\ell(s) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \cos\big(\mathbf{s}_\ell,\, f_\ell(s, i)\big)\]
Intuition: \(\text{SelfSim}\) tells us whether a word’s vector changes across sentences, while \(\text{IntraSim}\) tells us how that change shows up in space. If \(\text{SelfSim}\) is low but \(\text{IntraSim}\) is high, the model contextualizes crudely by pulling all words in the same sentence toward a shared sentence vector. If both \(\text{SelfSim}\) and \(\text{IntraSim}\) are low, every word gets a context-specific vector that still remains distinct from the other words in the same sentence.
3. Maximum explainable variance (\(\text{MEV}\)): Stack a word \(w\)’s representations across its \(n\) contexts as rows of an occurrence matrix \(\mathbf{X}_w = [f_\ell(s_1, i_1); \dots; f_\ell(s_n, i_n)]\), and let \(\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \dots \ge \sigma_m\) be its singular values. The maximum explainable variance is the fraction of total variance captured by the first principal component:
\[\text{MEV}_\ell(w) = \frac{\sigma_1^2}{\sum_{i} \sigma_i^2}\]
(For the step-by-step proof of why this ratio of squared singular values equals the maximum variance along a single 1D axis, see the MEV derivation page.)
Intuition: \(\text{MEV}\) puts an upper bound on how well a single static vector could approximate all of \(w\)’s contextualized vectors. If \(\text{MEV}_\ell(w) = 1\), all occurrences of \(w\) lie along a single line and one static embedding can replace them without loss. The closer \(\text{MEV}_\ell(w)\) is to 0, the more spread out \(w\)’s representations are across directions, and the worse any static replacement will be.


Adjusting for anisotropy
Raw similarity scores can be misleading when the underlying space is anisotropic. Suppose a layer is squeezed into such a narrow cone that any two random words have an average cosine similarity of \(0.99\). In that layer, observing \(\text{SelfSim}_\ell(w) = 0.95\) does not mean \(w\) is poorly contextualized, it means different occurrences of \(w\) are actually less similar to each other than two completely unrelated words picked at random.
To separate true contextualization from the background geometry of the cone, Ethayarajh computes a layer-specific anisotropic baseline (estimated over 1,000 uniformly randomly sampled word occurrences \(\mathcal{O}\)) and subtracts it from each raw metric:

For \(\text{SelfSim}\) and \(\text{IntraSim}\), the baseline is the expected cosine similarity between two randomly sampled words from different contexts in layer \(\ell\):

\[\text{Baseline}_{\text{cos}}(f_\ell) = \mathbb{E}_{x, y \sim \mathcal{U}(\mathcal{O})}\big[\cos(f_\ell(x), f_\ell(y))\big]\]
\[\text{SelfSim}^*_\ell(w) = \text{SelfSim}_\ell(w) - \text{Baseline}_{\text{cos}}(f_\ell)\] \[\text{IntraSim}^*_\ell(s) = \text{IntraSim}_\ell(s) - \text{Baseline}_{\text{cos}}(f_\ell)\]

For \(\text{MEV}\), the baseline is the proportion of variance explained by the first principal component of a matrix of uniformly randomly sampled word occurrences in layer \(\ell\) (with singular values \(\tilde{\sigma}_1 \ge \tilde{\sigma}_2 \ge \dots\)). When a layer sits in a narrow cone, a single direction already explains a large share of variance even for random words:

\[\text{Baseline}_{\text{MEV}}(f_\ell) = \frac{\tilde{\sigma}_1^2}{\sum_i \tilde{\sigma}_i^2}\] \[\text{MEV}^*_\ell(w) = \text{MEV}_\ell(w) - \text{Baseline}_{\text{MEV}}(f_\ell)\]


The findings
Using the anisotropy-adjusted metrics (\(\text{SelfSim}^*\), \(\text{IntraSim}^*\), and \(\text{MEV}^*\)) across all layers of ELMo, BERT, and GPT-2:
Finding 1: anisotropy is everywhere. In all hidden layers of all three models, \(\text{Baseline}_{\text{cos}}(f_\ell)\) is clearly above 0 (the sole exception is ELMo’s layer 0, which builds character-level vectors without context or position). Anisotropy generally increases with depth. In GPT-2 it sits around 0.6 in layers 2 to 8 and then climbs steeply; in the final layer, two random words have an average cosine similarity near 1. BERT also rises with depth, though its penultimate layer (layer 11) is noticeably more anisotropic than its final layer. Because hidden layers are almost always more anisotropic than layer 0, the paper suggests anisotropy is a by-product of contextualization itself.
Finding 2: upper layers are more context-specific (especially for stopwords). Adjusted self-similarity (\(\text{SelfSim}^*\)) drops steadily as layer depth increases across all three models, meaning upper layers produce representations that are much more specific to their context (with GPT-2’s final layer reaching near-zero \(\text{SelfSim}^*\)). Surprisingly, stopwords such as the, of, and to have the lowest self-similarity of all words, even though they are not polysemous. This rules out the idea that models merely assign each word one of a finite number of dictionary “sense” vectors; instead, the sheer variety of contexts a word appears in drives the variation in its representations.
Finding 3: context-specificity manifests differently per model. Adjusted intra-sentence similarity (\(\text{IntraSim}^*\)) diverges sharply across architectures:

ELMo: \(\text{IntraSim}^*\) rises in higher layers, meaning words in the same sentence are pulled closer together in vector space as they incorporate shared sentence context.
BERT: \(\text{IntraSim}^*\) generally drifts downward in upper layers (words in a sentence grow more distinct from each other), but stays positive (\(\approx 0.20\text{–}0.35\)), meaning words in the same sentence remain closer than random words (the baseline).
GPT-2: \(\text{IntraSim}^*\) is close to 0 across almost all hidden layers. Words in the same sentence are no more similar to each other than two random words from different sentences, showing that high contextualization does not require sentence words to converge toward a shared mean.

Finding 4: a single static vector explains less than 5% of variance. Across all layers of ELMo, BERT, and GPT-2, average adjusted maximum explainable variance (\(\text{MEV}^*\)) is below 5% (and for many words, raw \(\text{MEV}\) is smaller than the random-word baseline). Even in the best theoretical case (replacing with the first principal component), a static vector cannot approximate a word’s contextual representations. Still, if you extract static word embeddings by taking the first principal component of each word’s representations in the lower layers (especially BERT layer 1), they outperform GloVe and FastText on most traditional word-similarity and analogy benchmarks.

title: Anisotropy and Whitening: Fixing the Geometry of Embeddings
section: Why a cone hurts similarity search
text:
Why a cone hurts similarity search
Write each vector as the shared offset plus a residual: \(\mathbf{x} = \boldsymbol{\mu} + \mathbf{a}\), \(\mathbf{y} = \boldsymbol{\mu} + \mathbf{b}\). Then
\[
\mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{y} = \lVert\boldsymbol{\mu}\rVert^2 + \boldsymbol{\mu}\cdot(\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}) + \mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}.
\]
The informative part, how \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\) relate, is the last term. When \(\lVert\boldsymbol{\mu}\rVert\) is large, the first term dominates and every pair scores near 1: the meaningful differences are squeezed into a tiny range at the top of the scale. That makes scores fragile to noise and awkward to threshold. A fixed cutoff such as “keep results above 0.9” does not repair it, because what moved is the whole scale, not just where you cut it. Similarly, a few very-high-variance directions that carry non-semantic signal can dominate the dot product. Li et al. (2020), cited by Su et al., report for BERT sentence embeddings that word frequency biases the space.
To be precise about the claim: a narrow cone does not mathematically force the ranking to flip. If \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\cdot(\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b})\) were zero and the residuals had uniform norm and no noisy dominant directions, the \(\lVert\boldsymbol{\mu}\rVert^2\) term would just shift the dot product by a constant (and compress cosine similarity monotonically toward 1) without changing which pair is higher. The problem is that real embeddings are not that clean. The empirical evidence shows that raw BERT sentence embeddings compared with cosine do poorly on similarity benchmarks, and removing the anisotropy improves them.

title: Anisotropy and Whitening: Fixing the Geometry of Embeddings
text:
Whitening
Goal: transform the vectors so that their mean is 0 and their covariance matrix is the identity matrix \(\mathbf{I}\) (every direction has variance 1, and no direction is correlated with another). That is what a standard normal distribution looks like.

Intuition in two dimensions
Picture the points as a tilted, stretched ellipse.

Centre it: subtract the mean \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) so the cloud is around the origin (removes the shared offset).
Rotate it: rotate the axes to line up with the ellipse (this is what the eigenvectors \(\mathbf{U}\) of the covariance do). Now the coordinates are uncorrelated.
Rescale it: squash the long axis and stretch the short one so every axis has variance 1 (divide each by the square root of its variance, \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1/2}\)). The ellipse becomes a circle.






flowchart LR
    X["<b>Embeddings</b><br/>x ∈ ℝ<sup>d</sup><br/>N vectors"] --> M["<b>Centre</b><br/>x − μ"]
    M --> R["<b>Rotate to principal axes</b><br/>(x − μ) U"]
    R --> S["<b>Rescale each axis</b><br/>(x − μ) U Λ<sup>−1/2</sup><br/>divide axis j by √λⱼ"]
    S --> Z["<b>Whitened</b><br/>x̃ = (x − μ) W<br/>mean 0, covariance I"]
    S -. "keep first k columns of W" .-> K["<b>Whitening-k</b><br/>x̃ ∈ ℝ<sup>k</sup>, k < d"]








The formulas
Using the notation of Su et al. (row vectors; \(N\) embeddings \(\mathbf{x}_i \in \mathbb{R}^{1\times d}\)):
\[
\begin{gather*}
\boldsymbol{\mu} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbf{x}_i \qquad
\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol{\mu})^\top(\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol{\mu}) \\[6pt]
\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{U}^\top \quad\text{(SVD / eigendecomposition)} \qquad
\mathbf{W} = \mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1/2} \\[6pt]
\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_i = (\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu})\,\mathbf{W}
\end{gather*}
\]
Every symbol:

\(\boldsymbol{\mu}\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times d}\): the mean embedding. Subtracting it centres the data.
\(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\): the covariance matrix; entry \((j,k)\) says how coordinates \(j\) and \(k\) vary together (basically variance of \(\mathbf{x}_j\) and \(\mathbf{x}_k\)).
\(\mathbf{U}\): an orthogonal matrix whose columns are the principal directions (it rotates without stretching, so it preserves distances).
\(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\): a diagonal matrix of variances \(\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\dots\ge\lambda_d>0\) along those directions.
\(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1/2}\): the diagonal matrix with entries \(1/\sqrt{\lambda_j}\), i.e. “divide each axis by its standard deviation”.
\(\mathbf{W}\): the single \(d\times d\) matrix that does rotate-and-rescale; applying it is one matrix multiply.

In column-vector notation (used in some textbooks), the same transform reads \(\tilde{\mathbf{h}} = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1/2}\mathbf{U}^\top(\mathbf{h}-\boldsymbol{\mu})\); it is the transpose of the row form.
See the derivation page, for a step-by-step derivation of the whitening matrix, W.


Whitening-\(k\): shrinking the vectors
The values \(\lambda_j\) are sorted from largest to smallest. A direction with tiny \(\lambda_j\) barely varies, so it carries little information. Keeping only the first \(k\) columns of \(\mathbf{W}\) gives vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^{k}\):
\[
\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_i = (\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol{\mu})\,\mathbf{W}[:, :k]
\]
This is equivalent to PCA (keep the top directions) followed by the per-axis rescaling. Su et al. call it Whitening-\(k\). Because the cost of comparing two vectors grows with their dimension, a smaller \(k\) also means smaller storage and cheaper similarity computation.
\(k\) is a hyperparameter. Across most semantic similarity benchmarks evaluated by Su et al., reducing \(k\) to roughly a third of the original dimension \(d\) achieved near-optimal performance.


What it costs
You need \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) (\(1\times d\)) and \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) (\(d\times d\)) from a representative corpus of \(N\) vectors, a one-time computation of \(O(N\cdot d^2)\). Both can be accumulated incrementally in a single streaming pass (without storing the vectors); the memory needed is \(O(d^2)\) (does not grow with \(N\)). At query time whitening is one matrix multiply per vector.

title: Anisotropy and Whitening: Fixing the Geometry of Embeddings
text:
Try it: a NumPy demo
Synthetic data (our own), designed to be anisotropic: a large shared offset, three huge-variance directions that carry no topic information, and four “topics” hidden in small differences. We measure the average random-pair cosine and a retrieval-style score: for each vector, what fraction of its 10 nearest neighbours (by cosine) share its topic (P@10).
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
d, n_topics, per_topic = 64, 4, 250

# --- synthetic "anisotropic" embeddings -------------------------------------
# (1) a big shared offset: every vector leans the same way
common = rng.normal(size=d)
common *= 6.0 / np.linalg.norm(common)
# (2) three non-semantic directions with huge variance, the rest tiny
scales = np.concatenate([[4.0, 3.0, 2.0], np.full(d - 3, 0.15)])
# (3) the "semantics": topic centres, small in every direction
centres = rng.normal(size=(n_topics, d)) * 0.3
topic = np.repeat(np.arange(n_topics), per_topic)
X = common + centres[topic] + rng.normal(size=(len(topic), d)) * scales

def unit(A):
    return A / np.linalg.norm(A, axis=1, keepdims=True)

def mean_cosine(A):
    """Average cosine over all pairs of distinct rows."""
    S = unit(A) @ unit(A).T
    n = len(A)
    return float((S.sum() - n) / (n * (n - 1)))

def precision_at_10(Z):
    """Of each vector's 10 nearest neighbours (cosine), what fraction share its topic?"""
    S = unit(Z) @ unit(Z).T
    np.fill_diagonal(S, -np.inf)
    nn = np.argsort(-S, axis=1)[:, :10]
    return float((topic[nn] == topic[:, None]).mean())

def fit_whitening(X, k=None):
    """Su et al. notation (row vectors): x_tilde = (x - mu) @ W, with W = U Lambda^{-1/2}."""
    mu = X.mean(axis=0)
    Xc = X - mu
    cov = Xc.T @ Xc / len(X)             # Sigma = (1/N) sum (x-mu)^T (x-mu)
    U, lam, _ = np.linalg.svd(cov)       # Sigma = U diag(lam) U^T, lam sorted descending
    W = U / np.sqrt(lam)                 # scale column j of U by 1 / sqrt(lam_j)
    return mu, (W if k is None else W[:, :k])

mu, W = fit_whitening(X)
Xw = (X - mu) @ W

print(f"mean cosine, random pairs:  raw {mean_cosine(X):.3f} | whitened {mean_cosine(Xw):.3f}")
print(f"max |Cov(whitened) - I|:    {np.abs(np.cov(Xw, rowvar=False, bias=True) - np.eye(d)).max():.1e}")
print()
print(f"P@10 raw            {precision_at_10(X):.3f}")
print(f"P@10 centred only   {precision_at_10(X - mu):.3f}")
for k in (4, 8, 16, 32, 64):
    mu_k, W_k = fit_whitening(X, k)
    print(f"P@10 whitening-{k:<3}  {precision_at_10((X - mu_k) @ W_k):.3f}")
Output:
mean cosine, random pairs:  raw 0.539 | whitened -0.001
max |Cov(whitened) - I|:    6.2e-15

P@10 raw            0.968
P@10 centred only   0.975
P@10 whitening-4    0.707
P@10 whitening-8    1.000
P@10 whitening-16   0.954
P@10 whitening-32   0.744
P@10 whitening-64   0.563
What to notice:

The average random-pair cosine goes from 0.539 to about 0: isotropy restored, and the covariance of the whitened data is the identity to numerical precision.
On this toy data, the raw ranking is already good (P@10 0.968). Anisotropy does not automatically break retrieval; this matches the point made above.
Full whitening (\(k=64\)) made P@10 worse (0.563). Dividing by \(\sqrt{\lambda_j}\) blows up the directions with almost no variance, which here are mostly noise. Truncating to a small \(k\) fixed it (1.000 at \(k=8\)), and the best \(k\) is data-dependent. This is the same effect the paper’s \(k\)-sweep plots.

title: Anisotropy and Whitening: Fixing the Geometry of Embeddings
text:
Alternatives

All-but-the-top (Mu & Viswanath, 2018): subtract the mean and remove a few of the top principal directions.
BERT-flow (Li et al., 2020): learn an invertible neural network that maps the embedding distribution to a Gaussian.
Regularisation during training (Gao et al., 2019): penalise similarity between word embeddings so the cone widens.
Contrastive fine-tuning, for example SimCSE (Gao et al., 2021): train the encoder directly so that similar texts are close and others are spread out.

title: Anisotropy and Whitening: Fixing the Geometry of Embeddings
text:
Common pitfalls

Fit on a representative corpus. \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) and \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) describe your data. Statistics from a different domain can transfer worse.
Transform queries and documents identically. Fit \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) and \(\mathbf{W}\) once on your document corpus, apply that fixed transformation to both indexed documents and incoming queries.
Do not whiten blindly to full rank. Because whitening scales each principal axis by \(1/\sqrt{\lambda_j}\), tail directions with tiny variance (\(\lambda_j \ll 1\)) get massively amplified, turning numerical noise into dominant features. Treat \(k\) as a validation hyperparameter. Moreover, if you have fewer vectors than dimensions (\(N \le d\)), \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) is rank-deficient (\(\operatorname{rank}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}) \le N - 1\)) and cannot be inverted, meaning \(k\) must be strictly below the rank, or you must regularize the variances with a small constant \(\epsilon > 0\) (see Companion: Deriving the Whitening Matrix for the proof).
Expect uneven gains. Models already trained for similarity benefit less, and some datasets get worse.
Measure your own baseline. Compute the average random-pair cosine on your data before deciding it is a problem.

title: Companion: Principal Components, SVD, and Maximum Explainable Variance
text:
This page is a companion to Anisotropy and Whitening. It derives from scratch why the maximum explainable variance (MEV) along a single axis equals the ratio of squared singular values \(\sigma_1^2 / \sum_i \sigma_i^2\), and shows how singular values connect to the eigenvalues of \(\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X}\).
(Note on notation: in the main article and whitening derivation, \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) denotes the covariance matrix. Here we follow the standard SVD convention where \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) is the rectangular diagonal matrix of singular values \(\sigma_i\), and we write \(\mathbf{S}\) for the sample covariance matrix.)
crumbs: Companion: Principal Components, SVD, and Maximum Explainable Variance

title: Companion: Principal Components, SVD, and Maximum Explainable Variance
text:
Step 1: the centred data matrix
Let \(\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}\) be a data matrix of \(n\) observations (rows). For instance, \(n\) contextualized occurrences of a word \(w\) across \(d\) embedding dimensions (columns).
Before measuring variance, we mean-centre each column. Let \(\bar{x}_j = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n X_{ij}\) be the mean of column \(j\), and replace every entry \(X_{ij}\) with \(X_{ij} - \bar{x}_j\). After centring, the mean of every column of \(\mathbf{X}\) is zero.
crumbs: Companion: Principal Components, SVD, and Maximum Explainable Variance

title: Companion: Principal Components, SVD, and Maximum Explainable Variance
section: Step 2: deriving the exact sample covariance matrix
text:
Step 2: deriving the exact sample covariance matrix
The sample covariance between two coordinates (columns) \(j\) and \(k\) is defined as:
\[
S_{jk} = \frac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^n (X_{ij} - \bar{x}_j)(X_{ik} - \bar{x}_k).
\]
Because we centred \(\mathbf{X}\) in Step 1, \(\bar{x}_j = 0\) and \(\bar{x}_k = 0\), so this simplifies to:
\[
S_{jk} = \frac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^n X_{ij} X_{ik}.
\]
Notice that \(\sum_{i=1}^n X_{ij} X_{ik}\) is the dot product of column \(j\) and column \(k\) of \(\mathbf{X}\). Multiplying \(\mathbf{X}^\top\) (\(d \times n\)) by \(\mathbf{X}\) (\(n \times d\)) computes all column dot products at once. Therefore, the exact \(d \times d\) sample covariance matrix \(\mathbf{S}\) is:
\[
\mathbf{S} = \frac{1}{n-1} \mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X}.
\]
crumbs: Companion: Principal Components, SVD, and Maximum Explainable Variance

title: Companion: Principal Components, SVD, and Maximum Explainable Variance
section: Step 3: projecting the data onto a 1D axis
text:
Step 3: projecting the data onto a 1D axis
We want to compress our \(d\)-dimensional vectors onto a single 1D direction that retains as much spread as possible. Represent that direction by a unit column vector \(\mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times 1}\):
\[
\mathbf{v}^\top \mathbf{v} = 1.
\]
Projecting all \(n\) row vectors in \(\mathbf{X}\) onto \(\mathbf{v}\) is the matrix-vector product
\[
\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times 1},
\]
where \(z_i\) is the coordinate of the \(i\)-th observation along the axis \(\mathbf{v}\).
crumbs: Companion: Principal Components, SVD, and Maximum Explainable Variance

title: Companion: Principal Components, SVD, and Maximum Explainable Variance
section: Step 4: variance of the projected data
text:
Step 4: variance of the projected data
Because the columns of \(\mathbf{X}\) have mean zero, their linear combination \(\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{v}\) also has mean zero (\(\bar{z} = 0\)). The sample variance of the 1D projections \(z_1, \dots, z_n\) is therefore:
\[
\text{Var}(\mathbf{z}) = \frac{1}{n-1} \mathbf{z}^\top \mathbf{z}.
\]
Substitute \(\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{v}\):
\[
\text{Var}(\mathbf{z}) = \frac{1}{n-1} (\mathbf{X}\mathbf{v})^\top (\mathbf{X}\mathbf{v}) = \mathbf{v}^\top \left( \frac{1}{n-1} \mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X} \right) \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v}^\top \mathbf{S} \mathbf{v}.
\]
crumbs: Companion: Principal Components, SVD, and Maximum Explainable Variance

title: Companion: Principal Components, SVD, and Maximum Explainable Variance
section: Step 5: maximizing variance via Lagrange multipliers
text:
Step 5: maximizing variance via Lagrange multipliers
We want to choose \(\mathbf{v}\) to maximize \(\mathbf{v}^\top \mathbf{S} \mathbf{v}\) subject to the unit-length constraint \(\mathbf{v}^\top \mathbf{v} = 1\). Form the Lagrangian with multiplier \(\lambda\):
\[
\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{v}, \lambda) = \mathbf{v}^\top \mathbf{S} \mathbf{v} - \lambda(\mathbf{v}^\top \mathbf{v} - 1).
\]
Differentiate with respect to \(\mathbf{v}\) and set the gradient to \(\mathbf{0}\):
\[
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{v}} = 2\mathbf{S}\mathbf{v} - 2\lambda \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0} \implies \mathbf{S}\mathbf{v} = \lambda \mathbf{v}.
\]
This is the classic eigenvalue equation:

Any stationary direction \(\mathbf{v}\) must be an eigenvector of the covariance matrix \(\mathbf{S}\).
Left-multiplying both sides by \(\mathbf{v}^\top\) gives \(\mathbf{v}^\top \mathbf{S} \mathbf{v} = \lambda \mathbf{v}^\top \mathbf{v} = \lambda\).

Because \(\mathbf{v}^\top \mathbf{S} \mathbf{v}\) is the variance of the projected data from Step 4, the eigenvalue \(\lambda\) is the exact variance explained by the direction \(\mathbf{v}\). To capture the maximum possible variance along a single axis, we pick the eigenvector \(\mathbf{v}_1\) corresponding to the largest eigenvalue \(\lambda_1\). That vector is the first principal component, and the subsequent eigenvectors \(\mathbf{v}_2, \dots, \mathbf{v}_d\) (with \(\lambda_1 \ge \lambda_2 \ge \dots \ge \lambda_d \ge 0\)) capture the maximum remaining variance along orthogonal directions.
crumbs: Companion: Principal Components, SVD, and Maximum Explainable Variance

title: Companion: Principal Components, SVD, and Maximum Explainable Variance
section: Step 6: connecting SVD to the eigenvalues of \(\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X}\)
text:
Step 6: connecting SVD to the eigenvalues of \(\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X}\)
Any real matrix \(\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}\) has a Singular Value Decomposition (SVD):
\[
\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{V}^\top,
\]
where:

\(\mathbf{U} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}\) is orthogonal (\(\mathbf{U}^\top \mathbf{U} = \mathbf{I}_n\)), containing the left singular vectors as columns.
\(\boldsymbol{\Sigma} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}\) is rectangular diagonal with non-negative singular values \(\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \dots \ge 0\) along its main diagonal.
\(\mathbf{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}\) is orthogonal (\(\mathbf{V}^\top \mathbf{V} = \mathbf{V}\mathbf{V}^\top = \mathbf{I}_d\)), containing the right singular vectors as columns.

Substitute \(\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{V}^\top\) into \(\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X}\):
\[
\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X} = (\mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{V}^\top)^\top (\mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{V}^\top) = \mathbf{V}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^\top \underbrace{\mathbf{U}^\top \mathbf{U}}_{\mathbf{I}_n} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{V}^\top = \mathbf{V}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma})\mathbf{V}^\top.
\]
Here \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) is a \(d \times d\) diagonal matrix whose \(i\)-th diagonal entry is \(\sigma_i^2\). Right-multiplying both sides by \(\mathbf{V}\) (and using \(\mathbf{V}^\top \mathbf{V} = \mathbf{I}_d\)) gives:
\[
(\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X})\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{V}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}), \qquad\text{or column by column:}\qquad (\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X})\mathbf{v}_i = \sigma_i^2 \mathbf{v}_i.
\]
Dividing by \(n - 1\) links this directly to our covariance matrix \(\mathbf{S} = \frac{1}{n-1}\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X}\):
\[
\mathbf{S}\mathbf{v}_i = \left(\frac{\sigma_i^2}{n-1}\right)\mathbf{v}_i.
\]
Comparing this with \(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{v}_i = \lambda_i \mathbf{v}_i\) from Step 5 gives two fundamental identities:

Principal components are right singular vectors: the columns \(\mathbf{v}_i\) of \(\mathbf{V}\) are the exact eigenvectors of \(\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X}\) and of \(\mathbf{S}\).
Singular values vs. eigenvalues: the squared singular values \(\sigma_i^2\) of \(\mathbf{X}\) are the eigenvalues of \(\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X}\), and the variance explained by the \(i\)-th principal component is \(\lambda_i = \frac{\sigma_i^2}{n-1}\).
crumbs: Companion: Principal Components, SVD, and Maximum Explainable Variance

title: Companion: Principal Components, SVD, and Maximum Explainable Variance
section: Step 7: the Maximum Explainable Variance (MEV) formula
text:
Step 7: the Maximum Explainable Variance (MEV) formula
The proportion of total variance explained by the first \(k\) principal components is the sum of the first \(k\) variances divided by the total variance across all directions:
\[
\text{Explained Variance Ratio}(k) = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^k \lambda_i}{\sum_{i=1}^d \lambda_i} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^k \frac{\sigma_i^2}{n-1}}{\sum_{i=1}^d \frac{\sigma_i^2}{n-1}} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^k \sigma_i^2}{\sum_{i=1}^d \sigma_i^2}.
\]
Setting \(k = 1\) gives the exact proportion of variance captured by the single best 1D axis, which is Ethayarajh’s (2019) maximum explainable variance:
\[
\text{MEV} = \frac{\sigma_1^2}{\sum_{i} \sigma_i^2}.
\]

title: Companion: From Corpus Log-Likelihood to the WordPiece Merge Score
text:
This is a companion mathematical note to Tokenization and Byte-Pair Encoding: How LLMs Turn Text into Numbers.
When building a subword vocabulary bottom-up, Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) merges whichever adjacent pair \((a, b)\) has the highest raw count \(\text{count}(ab)\). WordPiece (Schuster & Nakajima, 2012; Devlin et al., 2019) instead chooses the merge that best improves the log-likelihood of the training corpus.
In many tutorials, you will usually see two different formulas for WordPiece:
Two questions naturally arise when looking at these equations:
Below is the complete derivation answering both questions from first principles.
crumbs: Companion: From Corpus Log-Likelihood to the WordPiece Merge Score

title: Companion: From Corpus Log-Likelihood to the WordPiece Merge Score
text:
1. The Unigram Log-Likelihood Setup
Suppose our training corpus currently consists of a sequence of \(N\) tokens \(t_1, t_2, \dots, t_N\) drawn from a vocabulary \(V\).
To score how well the vocabulary \(V\) models the corpus, WordPiece fits a unigram language model: it assumes every token occurs independently with its maximum-likelihood probability \(P(t) = \frac{c_t}{N}\), where \(c_t = \text{count}(t)\) is the number of times token \(t\) appears in the corpus.
The total log-likelihood of the corpus is:
\[\log L = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \log P(t_i) = \sum_{t \in V} c_t \log \left(\frac{c_t}{N}\right) = \left(\sum_{t \in V} c_t \log c_t\right) - N \log N\]
Now suppose we consider merging every adjacent pair \((a, b)\) (assuming \(a \neq b\)) into a single new token \(ab\), which occurs \(c_{ab} = \text{count}(ab)\) times. Look carefully at what happens to the corpus statistics before and after the merge:








Quantity
Before Merge (\(\log L_{\text{old}}\))
After Merge (\(\log L_{\text{new}}\))




Total tokens in corpus
\(N\)
\(N' = N - c_{ab}\)


Count of merged token \(ab\)
\(0\)
\(c_{ab}\)


Count of standalone \(a\)
\(c_a\)
\(c'_a = c_a - c_{ab}\)


Count of standalone \(b\)
\(c_b\)
\(c'_b = c_b - c_{ab}\)


Count of any other token \(t \notin \{a, b, ab\}\)
\(c_t\)
\(c_t\) (unchanged)



Notice that merging \((a, b) \to ab\) does not just replace \(c_{ab}\) pairs of \((a, b)\) in isolation:

Leftover \(a\)’s and \(b\)’s lose probability mass: Any unmerged instances of \(a\) and \(b\) sitting elsewhere in the corpus see their counts drop from \(c_a \to c_a - c_{ab}\) and \(c_b \to c_b - c_{ab}\).
The entire corpus shrinks: Every merged pair reduces the total token count of the corpus by \(1\), shrinking the corpus size from \(N\) to \(N - c_{ab}\) and slightly boosting the probability \(\frac{c_t}{N - c_{ab}}\) of every other token in the vocabulary.
crumbs: Companion: From Corpus Log-Likelihood to the WordPiece Merge Score

title: Companion: From Corpus Log-Likelihood to the WordPiece Merge Score
text:
2. The Exact Log-Likelihood Change (\(\Delta \log L\))
Let us compute the exact difference \(\Delta \log L = \log L_{\text{new}} - \log L_{\text{old}}\). When we subtract \(\log L_{\text{old}}\) from \(\log L_{\text{new}}\), the \(c_t \log c_t\) terms for all unrelated tokens (\(t \notin \{a, b, ab\}\)) cancel out completely because their counts do not change:
\[\Delta \log L = c_{ab} \log c_{ab} + (c_a - c_{ab})\log(c_a - c_{ab}) + (c_b - c_{ab})\log(c_b - c_{ab}) - c_a \log c_a - c_b \log c_b - (N - c_{ab})\log(N - c_{ab}) + N \log N\]
By splitting \(c_a = c_{ab} + (c_a - c_{ab})\), \(c_b = c_{ab} + (c_b - c_{ab})\), and \(N = c_{ab} + (N - c_{ab})\), we can rearrange this exact equality into three interpretable pieces:
\[\Delta \log L = \underbrace{c_{ab} \log \left( \frac{N \cdot c_{ab}}{c_a \, c_b} \right)}_{\text{Term 1: Primary PMI Gain}} + \underbrace{(c_a - c_{ab}) \log \left( 1 - \frac{c_{ab}}{c_a} \right) + (c_b - c_{ab}) \log \left( 1 - \frac{c_{ab}}{c_b} \right)}_{\text{Term 2: Penalty on leftover } a\text{'s and } b\text{'s}} - \underbrace{(N - c_{ab}) \log \left( 1 - \frac{c_{ab}}{N} \right)}_{\text{Term 3: Corpus shrinkage boost}}\]

Numerical Verification on a Toy Corpus
Suppose \(N = 1000\), \(c_a = 100\), \(c_b = 100\), and \(c_{ab} = 50\) (using natural logarithms \(\ln\)):

Term 1 (Textbook approximation): \(50 \ln\left(\frac{1000 \cdot 50}{100 \cdot 100}\right) = 50 \ln(5) \approx \mathbf{+80.47}\)
Term 2 (Leftover \(a\) and \(b\) penalty): \(50 \ln(1 - 0.5) + 50 \ln(1 - 0.5) = 100 \ln(0.5) \approx \mathbf{-69.31}\)
Term 3 (Corpus shrinkage boost from \(N=1000 \to 950\)): \(-950 \ln(1 - 0.05) \approx \mathbf{+48.73}\)
Exact \(\Delta \log L\): \(80.47 - 69.31 + 48.73 = \mathbf{+59.89}\)

Notice how Term 2 (negative) and Term 3 (positive) pull in opposite directions and partially cancel each other out.
crumbs: Companion: From Corpus Log-Likelihood to the WordPiece Merge Score

title: Companion: From Corpus Log-Likelihood to the WordPiece Merge Score
section: 3. Why Terms 2 and 3 Can Be Ignored (First-Order Taylor Expansion)
text:
3. Why Terms 2 and 3 Can Be Ignored (First-Order Taylor Expansion)
To see why Term 1 dominates in any realistic training corpus, we apply the first-order Taylor expansion for natural logarithms around \(x = 0\):
\[\ln(1 - x) \approx -x \quad \text{for small } x\]

Expanding Term 3 (The Corpus Shrinkage Boost)
In a real training corpus, \(N\) is in the millions or billions while the count of any single candidate pair \(c_{ab}\) is small relative to \(N\) (\(c_{ab} \ll N\)). Setting \(x = \frac{c_{ab}}{N}\) gives:
\[-(N - c_{ab}) \ln \left( 1 - \frac{c_{ab}}{N} \right) \approx -(N - c_{ab}) \left( -\frac{c_{ab}}{N} \right) = c_{ab} - \frac{c_{ab}^2}{N} \approx \mathbf{+c_{ab}}\]


Expanding Term 2 (The Leftover \(a\) and \(b\) Penalty)
Consider the penalty for leftover standalone \(a\)’s, \((c_a - c_{ab}) \ln \left( 1 - \frac{c_{ab}}{c_a} \right)\), across its two boundary regimes:

When \(c_{ab} \ll c_a\): Applying \(\ln(1 - \frac{c_{ab}}{c_a}) \approx -\frac{c_{ab}}{c_a}\) gives \((c_a - c_{ab})(-\frac{c_{ab}}{c_a}) \approx \mathbf{-c_{ab}}\) (and similarly \(\mathbf{-c_{ab}}\) for \(b\)).
When \(c_{ab} \to c_a\): Almost every instance of \(a\) is absorbed into \(ab\), so \((c_a - c_{ab}) \to 0\) and the penalty vanishes to \(\mathbf{0}\).

Across the entire valid domain \(0 \le c_{ab} \le \min(c_a, c_b)\), the combined penalty in Term 2 is strictly bounded between \(-2c_{ab}\) and \(0\).


Dominant Balance
Summing Term 2 (\(\in [-2c_{ab}, 0]\)) and Term 3 (\(\approx +c_{ab}\)) produces a net linear correction bounded inside \([-c_{ab}, +c_{ab}]\). Factoring \(c_{ab}\) out of the entire exact equation yields:
\[\Delta \log L = c_{ab} \cdot \left[ \underbrace{\ln \left( \frac{N \cdot c_{ab}}{c_a \, c_b} \right)}_{\text{PMI of } a \text{ and } b} + \underbrace{\mathcal{O}(1)}_{\text{bounded in } [-1,\,+1]} \right]\]
Because \(N\) is massive, the logarithmic ratio \(\ln\left(\frac{N \cdot c_{ab}}{c_a c_b}\right) = \ln \frac{P(ab)}{P(a)P(b)}\) dominates the bounded \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) offset. Dropping that offset gives the classic first-order approximation:
\[\Delta \log L \approx c_{ab} \cdot \log \frac{P(ab)}{P(a)\,P(b)}\]
crumbs: Companion: From Corpus Log-Likelihood to the WordPiece Merge Score

title: Companion: From Corpus Log-Likelihood to the WordPiece Merge Score
section: 4. From Total Gain to the Simplified Score (Average Gain per Occurrence)
text:
4. From Total Gain to the Simplified Score (Average Gain per Occurrence)
If we rank candidate merges directly by \(\Delta \log L \approx c_{ab} \cdot \log \frac{P(ab)}{P(a)P(b)}\), notice that \(c_{ab}\) sits outside the logarithm as a linear multiplier. Because a linear factor grows much faster than a logarithm, raw pair frequency (\(c_{ab}\)) will still dominate the ranking making the merge order behave almost identically to BPE.
Furthermore, as long as \(c_{ab}\) sits in front of the logarithm, we cannot algebraically drop the \(\log\) or \(N\), because bringing \(c_{ab}\) inside the logarithm turns it into an exponent: \(\log\left(\left(\frac{N \cdot c_{ab}}{c_a c_b}\right)^{c_{ab}}\right)\).
Instead, simplified WordPiece shifts the objective from total corpus log-likelihood gain (\(\Delta \log L\)) to average log-likelihood gain per merge occurrence by dividing both sides by \(c_{ab}\):
\[\frac{\Delta \log L}{c_{ab}} \approx \log \frac{P(ab)}{P(a)\,P(b)}\]
In information theory, this quantity is the Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI) between \(a\) and \(b\). Substituting \(P(t) = \frac{c_t}{N}\) gives:
\[\frac{\Delta \log L}{c_{ab}} \approx \log \left( N \cdot \frac{c_{ab}}{c_a \, c_b} \right)\]
Now we can apply two lossless monotonic simplifications to rank candidate pairs:

Drop \(\log(\cdot)\): Because the logarithm is a strictly increasing function, \(\log(x_1) > \log(x_2) \iff x_1 > x_2\) for all positive \(x_1, x_2\).
Drop \(N\): At any given step of the merge loop, the total token count \(N\) is an identical positive constant for every candidate pair \((a, b)\).

Stripping away \(\log\) and \(N\) preserves the exact ranking order of \(\frac{\Delta \log L}{c_{ab}}\) and yields the standard WordPiece scoring rule:
\[\text{score}(a,b) = \frac{c_{ab}}{c_a \cdot c_b} = \frac{\text{count}(ab)}{\text{count}(a) \cdot \text{count}(b)}\]

title: Masks, Cross-Attention and the Original Transformer
text:
This is Part 5, the second of four articles on attention. Part 4 built scaled dot-product attention:
\[
\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V
\]
Here we use it in three ways, following the original Transformer paper (Vaswani et al., 2017): bidirectional self-attention, masked self-attention, and cross-attention. Then we see which parts modern LLMs kept.

title: Masks, Cross-Attention and the Original Transformer
text:
The original job: translation
The Transformer was introduced for sequence-to-sequence tasks such as machine translation. Two stacks of layers do two different jobs:

The encoder reads the whole source sentence and produces one contextual vector per source token.
The decoder writes the output sentence one token at a time, consulting the encoder’s output as it goes.




The original encoder-decoder Transformer (drawn for this article). Orange arrows show the encoder output used as keys and values in cross-attention.


A few facts from the paper that the figure encodes (Vaswani et al., 2017):

Both stacks have \(N = 6\) identical layers, and every sub-layer and embedding outputs vectors of size \(d_\text{model} = 512\).
Each sub-layer is wrapped as \(\text{LayerNorm}(x + \text{Sublayer}(x))\): add the sub-layer’s input back (a residual connection), then normalize.
An encoder layer has two sub-layers: self-attention and a feed-forward network.
A decoder layer has three: masked self-attention, cross-attention over the encoder output, and a feed-forward network.
The input embeddings get positional encodings added, because attention alone has no sense of order. That is the topic of a later article.

title: Masks, Cross-Attention and the Original Transformer
section: The encoder: every token sees every token
text:
The encoder: every token sees every token
In encoder self-attention, queries, keys and values all come from the previous layer’s output, and each position can attend to all positions. No mask is applied, so information flows in both directions. If you translate “the bank of the river”, the encoder’s vector for “bank” can use “river”, which comes later in the sentence.

title: Masks, Cross-Attention and the Original Transformer
section: The decoder, part 1: the causal mask
text:
The decoder, part 1: the causal mask
The decoder produces the output one token at a time, and token \(t\) may depend only on tokens before it. If the decoder could peek at the answer while predicting it, training would be trivial and useless.
The fix is a causal mask \(M\) added to the scores before the softmax:
\[
\text{MaskedAttn}(Q,K,V) = \text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}} + M\right)V,
\qquad
M_{ij} = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } j \le i \quad(\text{allowed}) \\ -\infty & \text{if } j > i \quad(\text{future token}) \end{cases}
\]
Here \(i\) is the query position (the row) and \(j\) is the key position (the column). The paper describes this as setting to \(-\infty\) the softmax inputs that correspond to illegal connections (Vaswani et al., 2017). A concrete 4-token example, with scores that are already scaled:
\[
S = \begin{pmatrix} 2&1&0&1\\ 0&2&1&0\\ 1&0&2&1\\ 0&1&1&2 \end{pmatrix}
\qquad
S + M = \begin{pmatrix} 2&-\infty&-\infty&-\infty\\ 0&2&-\infty&-\infty\\ 1&0&2&-\infty\\ 0&1&1&2 \end{pmatrix}
\]
\[
\text{softmax}(S + M) \approx \begin{pmatrix} 1&0&0&0\\ 0.119&0.881&0&0\\ 0.245&0.090&0.665&0\\ 0.072&0.197&0.197&0.534 \end{pmatrix}
\]
Row \(i\) is a proper probability distribution over positions \(1, \dots, i\) only. The result is a lower-triangular attention matrix.
Why \(-\infty\) and not 0? Adding 0 changes nothing: the score stays what it was, and the token still gets weight. In the example above, without the mask the first token would put \(0.197 + 0.072 + 0.197 = 47\%\) of its attention on tokens 2, 3 and 4. Since softmax computes \(e^{s}\), a score of \(-\infty\) gives \(e^{-\infty} = 0\) exactly, and the remaining weights renormalize to sum to 1.





flowchart LR
  A["<b>Scores</b><br/>S = QKᵀ/√d_k (n×n)"] --> B["<b>Add mask</b><br/>S + M<br/>M = −∞ above the diagonal"]
  B --> C["<b>Softmax per row</b><br/>future weights become exactly 0"]
  C --> D["<b>Weighted sum</b><br/>O = A·V"]






import numpy as np

def softmax(z, axis=-1):
    z = z - z.max(axis=axis, keepdims=True)
    e = np.exp(z)
    return e / e.sum(axis=axis, keepdims=True)

def causal_mask(n):
    # 0 on and below the diagonal, -inf above it
    return np.triu(np.full((n, n), -np.inf), k=1)

def masked_attention(Q, K, V):
    n, d_k = Q.shape
    scores = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(d_k) + causal_mask(n)   # add the mask BEFORE softmax
    weights = softmax(scores)
    return weights @ V, weights

title: Masks, Cross-Attention and the Original Transformer
section: The decoder, part 2: teacher forcing and the right shift
text:
The decoder, part 2: teacher forcing and the right shift
During training, we already know the full target sentence. Instead of generating token by token, the decoder processes the entire target in one parallel pass, and the causal mask ensures every position still behaves as if it were generating step by step. Feeding the true previous tokens (rather than the model’s own predictions) is called teacher forcing. It is what makes training parallel and fast.
There is a subtlety. The mask allows \(j \le i\), which includes the diagonal: position \(i\) may look at itself. If the decoder input at position \(i\) were the very token \(y_i\) it is supposed to predict, it could simply copy it. The paper’s fix is to offset the output embeddings by one position (the “outputs, shifted right” at the bottom of the figure). Together, the mask and the shift guarantee that the prediction at position \(i\) depends only on known outputs at positions less than \(i\) (Vaswani et al., 2017).
tokens = ["<bos>", "Los", "gatos", "duermen", "<eos>"]
decoder_input  = tokens[:-1]   # <bos> Los gatos duermen
decoder_target = tokens[1:]    # Los gatos duermen <eos>

Read the table row by row: the mask hides everything to the right, and the shift makes sure the token at position \(t\) is the previous target, not the one being predicted.
At inference there is no known target. The model generates one token, appends it to the input, and repeats, so the mask is implicit in the process. (During the first pass over a long prompt, all prompt tokens are processed in parallel, so the causal mask is still needed there.) One consequence of teacher forcing is that the model is trained on true prefixes but run on its own outputs; this train/test mismatch is often called exposure bias.

title: Masks, Cross-Attention and the Original Transformer
text:
The decoder, part 3: cross-attention
After masked self-attention, each decoder layer has a second attention sub-layer that lets the decoder “read” the source sentence. In cross-attention:

The queries come from the decoder (the previous sub-layer’s output).
The keys and values come from the encoder’s final output \(H_\text{enc}\).
No causal mask is applied: every decoder position can attend to every source position.

\[
\text{CrossAttn}(Q_\text{dec}, K_\text{enc}, V_\text{enc}) = \text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{Q_\text{dec} K_\text{enc}^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V_\text{enc}
\]
If the source has \(n\) tokens and the target so far has \(m\), then \(Q_\text{dec} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times d_k}\) and \(K_\text{enc}, V_\text{enc} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_k}\), so the score matrix is \(m \times n\): one row per output position, one column per source token. It is rectangular, unlike self-attention’s square matrix.
For illustration: when a decoder is about to produce the Spanish word “gatos”, we would expect cross-attention to put much of its weight on the source token “cats”. That is the decoder dynamically deciding which part of the input matters for this output step.
The paper uses multi-head attention in exactly three ways (Vaswani et al., 2017):
