title: Masks, Cross-Attention and the Original Transformer
text:
From encoder-decoder to decoder-only
Modern LLMs such as GPT-style models, Llama, Mistral and Qwen use only the decoder, with the encoder and the cross-attention sub-layer removed.



A decoder-only (GPT-style) block with the Pre-Norm layout used by most modern LLMs (drawn for this article).


What changes:

One sequence, one stack. The prompt and the continuation are a single token sequence. The same causal mask handles both: prompt tokens attend to earlier prompt tokens, and generated tokens attend to everything before them.
No cross-attention. There is no separate source to read from. Everything the model knows about the input is in the same sequence it is extending.
One objective. Training is plain next-token prediction on text, with every position in a sequence providing a training signal.

Commonly cited reasons for the shift are simplicity (one model, one loss), and that the pretraining objective matches how the model is used at generation time. These are explanations from later work and practice rather than claims of the original paper, and encoder-decoder models are still used, particularly for tasks with a clearly separate input and output such as translation and summarization. Cross-attention also lives on in multimodal models, where an image encoder can supply keys and values to a language decoder.

A note on the two diagrams. The original design applies layer normalization after the residual addition (Post-Norm: \(\text{LayerNorm}(x + \text{Sublayer}(x))\)). Most modern decoder-only LLMs apply it before the sub-layer (Pre-Norm: \(x + \text{Sublayer}(\text{LayerNorm}(x))\)). Why that matters is the subject of a later article in this series.

title: Masks, Cross-Attention and the Original Transformer
text:
Common pitfalls

Adding the mask in the wrong place. The mask is added to the scores before softmax. Multiplying the weights by 0 after softmax leaves rows that no longer sum to 1.
Forgetting the shift. If decoder inputs are not shifted relative to the targets, position \(i\) sees the token it must predict. Training loss collapses toward zero and the model produces garbage at inference, because it learned to copy.
Confusing padding masks with causal masks. They solve different problems: a padding mask hides padding tokens in a batch, a causal mask hides future tokens. Real code often needs both, combined.
Fully masked rows. If every entry in a row is \(-\infty\), softmax computes \(0/0\) and returns NaN (try softmax(np.full((1, 3), -np.inf))). Make sure every query has at least one allowed key, and in low-precision floats prefer the dtype’s most negative finite value over a literal infinity.
Mixing up cross-attention sources. Queries come from the decoder; keys and values come only from the encoder output. Swapping them changes what the layer computes.
Believing the mask only matters in training. It also matters at inference whenever several tokens are processed in parallel, for example when a long prompt is first fed through the model.

title: Masks, Cross-Attention and the Original Transformer
text:
Summary

The original Transformer has an encoder (bidirectional self-attention) and a decoder (masked self-attention, then cross-attention, then a feed-forward network).
The causal mask adds \(-\infty\) above the diagonal of the score matrix, so future positions get exactly zero weight.
The right shift of the decoder input prevents each position from seeing its own target; the mask prevents it from seeing later ones. Together they allow parallel training with teacher forcing.
Cross-attention takes queries from the decoder and keys and values from the encoder output, with no causal mask.
Decoder-only LLMs keep the masked self-attention stack and drop the encoder and cross-attention.

title: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE)
text: Part 8 showed why attention needs position information and covered the classic methods. Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE; Su et al., 2021, the “RoFormer” paper) is the method most modern open LLM families build on; the YaRN paper lists the LLaMA, GPT-NeoX and PaLM families as RoPE models. The idea fits in one sentence: rotate each query and key by an angle proportional to its position, and the dot product between them then automatically depends on how far apart they are.

title: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE)
text:
1. The goal
Write the position-aware query and key as \(f_q(x_m, m)\) and \(f_k(x_n, n)\), where \(x_m, x_n\) are the embeddings of the tokens at positions \(m\) and \(n\). We want their inner product to depend on the two contents and on the relative offset only:
\[
\langle f_q(x_m, m),\, f_k(x_n, n)\rangle = g(x_m, x_n, m-n)
\]
\(g\) is just “some function of those three things”. Why relative? A phrase should behave the same whether it sits at position 5 or at position 5000, and attention between two words should depend on how far apart they are, not on where in the document they happen to be.

title: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE)
text:
2. The idea in 2D
Start with a query and a key that are 2-dimensional. The dot product of two vectors is \(|a||b|\cos(\text{angle between them})\). It only cares about the lengths and the angle between the vectors.
So: rotate the query by \(m\theta\) and the key by \(n\theta\), where \(\theta\) is a fixed angle. Rotations do not change lengths. The angle between the rotated vectors is the original angle plus \((n-m)\theta\). Shift both positions by the same amount and nothing changes.



Two positions with the same offset \(n-m=1\) give the same angle between \(q'\) and \(k'\).


In symbols, with the rotation matrix \(R(\alpha) = \begin{pmatrix}\cos\alpha & -\sin\alpha\\ \sin\alpha & \cos\alpha\end{pmatrix}\):
\[
\tilde q_m = R(m\theta)\,W_q x_m, \qquad
\tilde k_n = R(n\theta)\,W_k x_n
\]
\(W_q, W_k\) are the usual learned projections; \(\theta\) is a fixed constant; \(\tilde q_m,\tilde k_n\) are the position-encoded query and key. Their dot product is
\[
\tilde q_m^\top \tilde k_n
= (W_q x_m)^\top R(m\theta)^\top R(n\theta)\,(W_k x_n)
= (W_q x_m)^\top R\big((n-m)\theta\big)\,(W_k x_n)
\]
The middle step uses two facts about rotations: \(R(\alpha)^\top = R(-\alpha)\) and \(R(\alpha)R(\beta) = R(\alpha+\beta)\). The absolute positions \(m\) and \(n\) have disappeared; only \(n-m\) survives.
The RoFormer paper derives this as a solution of the requirement in Section 1, using complex numbers. The full derivation, including the assumptions it makes, is on the companion page.

title: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE)
text:
3. From 2D to \(d\) dimensions
Real queries have \(d\) dimensions (the head dimension, often 64 or 128). RoPE splits them into \(d/2\) pairs \((x^{(1)},x^{(2)}), (x^{(3)},x^{(4)}),\dots\) and rotates each pair as its own 2D plane, each with its own angle:
\[
\theta_i = 10000^{-2i/d}, \qquad i = 0, 1, \dots, \tfrac d2 - 1
\]
(The paper indexes \(i\) from 1 and writes \(10000^{-2(i-1)/d}\); it is the same set of values.) At position \(m\) pair \(i\) is rotated by \(m\theta_i\). As a matrix, this is block-diagonal:
\[
R^d_{\Theta,m} = \begin{pmatrix}
R(m\theta_0) & & \\
& R(m\theta_1) & \\
& & \ddots
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\tilde q_m^\top \tilde k_n = x_m^\top W_q^\top\, R^d_{\Theta,\,n-m}\, W_k x_n
\]
Because each block is a rotation, \(R^d_{\Theta,m}\) is orthogonal: it preserves the norm of \(q\) and \(k\), so RoPE does not change the scale of the scores. It adds no parameters. \(d\) must be even.
Efficient form. Building the full matrix wastes work because it is mostly zeros. Rotating a pair \((a,b)\) by \(\alpha\) gives \((a\cos\alpha - b\sin\alpha,\ a\sin\alpha + b\cos\alpha)\), which is \((a,b)\cos\alpha + (-b,a)\sin\alpha\). For the whole vector:
\[
R^d_{\Theta,m}\,x = x \odot \begin{pmatrix}\cos m\theta_0\\ \cos m\theta_0\\ \cos m\theta_1\\ \cos m\theta_1\\ \vdots\end{pmatrix}
+ \begin{pmatrix}-x^{(2)}\\ x^{(1)}\\ -x^{(4)}\\ x^{(3)}\\ \vdots\end{pmatrix} \odot \begin{pmatrix}\sin m\theta_0\\ \sin m\theta_0\\ \sin m\theta_1\\ \sin m\theta_1\\ \vdots\end{pmatrix}
\]
where \(\odot\) is element-wise multiplication. This is a couple of element-wise operations on \(x\), with the cos and sin tables computed once.

title: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE)
section: 4. Where RoPE is applied, and why only there
text:
4. Where RoPE is applied, and why only there





flowchart LR
  X["<b>Token embedding</b><br/>xₘ"] --> Q["<b>Query</b><br/>W_q xₘ"] --> RQ["<b>Rotate by position</b><br/>q̃ₘ = R_{Θ,m} W_q xₘ"]
  X --> K["<b>Key</b><br/>W_k xₘ"] --> RK["<b>Rotate by position</b><br/>k̃ₘ = R_{Θ,m} W_k xₘ"]
  X --> V["<b>Value</b><br/>vₘ = W_v xₘ<br/>(not rotated)"]
  RQ --> S["<b>Scores</b><br/>q̃ₘᵀ k̃ₙ / √d"]
  RK --> S
  S --> O["<b>Output</b><br/>oₘ = Σₙ aₘₙ vₙ"]
  V --> O






RoPE rotates the query and key only, after their projections, inside every attention layer. Three reasons:

It must act right before the dot product. The collapse to \(R_{n-m}\) needs the rotations to sit directly between \(W_q x_m\) and \(W_k x_n\). If you rotated the input embedding instead, you would get \(x_m^\top R_m^\top W_q^\top W_k R_n x_n\), and because \(W_q^\top W_k\) does not generally commute with a rotation, no relative-only form comes out.
Values do not take part in the score. Position should decide how much token \(n\) contributes to token \(m\) (the weight \(a_{mn}\)), not rotate what it contributes. If \(v_n\) were rotated by its absolute position, the layer’s output would pick up absolute-position dependence, which works against the relative-only design. In the RoFormer paper the values stay as \(W_v x_n\).
Every layer gets fresh position information. Additive encodings enter once at the input and have to survive through all the layers. RoPE re-applies the rotation to the new \(q\) and \(k\) in each layer.

title: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE)
section: 5. What do the different frequencies do?
text:
5. What do the different frequencies do?
Pair \(i\) rotates by \(\theta_i\) radians per token, so it completes a full turn every \(\lambda_i = 2\pi/\theta_i = 2\pi\cdot 10000^{2i/d}\) tokens. These are the same geometric frequencies as the sinusoidal encoding of Part 1, now applied by rotation to \(q\) and \(k\). For a head dimension \(d=128\):

pair \(0\) turns every \(2\pi\approx 6.3\) tokens (about one radian per token);
pair \(63\) (the slowest) turns every \(\approx 54{,}000\) tokens.

Think of the hands of a clock. Fast pairs tell nearby offsets apart precisely, but they wrap around, so at long range a fast pair’s angle is ambiguous. Slow pairs barely move across a few tokens, but their angle changes steadily over thousands of tokens, which gives a coarse sense of large distances. Part 3 builds on this: extending context windows is mostly about what to do with the slow pairs.

title: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE)
section: 6. Long-term decay: what the paper claims, precisely
text:
6. Long-term decay: what the paper claims, precisely
The paper states that with \(\theta_i = 10000^{-2i/d}\) the inner product has a long-term decay: the dependence between tokens shrinks as their relative distance grows. The argument bounds the score by an expression involving \(\frac{2}{d}\sum_j |S_j|\), where \(S_j=\sum_{l<j}e^{\mathrm{i}(m-n)\theta_l}\) is a sum of unit complex numbers rotating at the pair frequencies. The paper then shows numerically that this average shrinks (with oscillations) as \(|m-n|\) grows.
Two honest qualifiers. This is a bound on a proxy, not a statement that every attention weight decays with distance. A model can learn to concentrate its query and key energy in slow pairs and attend far away. And the paper’s own limitations section says the authors do not have a faithful explanation for why RoPE converges faster, or does better on long texts, than the baselines. Details and our own plot of the proxy are on the companion page.

title: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE)
text:
7. Compatibility with linear attention
Standard attention computes all \(N^2\) query-key scores. Linear attention (Katharopoulos et al., 2020) replaces \(\exp(q^\top k/\sqrt d)\) by a kernel \(\phi(q)^\top\varphi(k)\) with non-negative feature maps \(\phi,\varphi\). Then the sum \(\sum_n \varphi(k_n)v_n^\top\) can be computed once and reused for every query, giving \(O(N)\) cost.
Additive position encodings and relative biases put position inside the pairwise score, which does not factor into a separate function of \(q\) and of \(k\). RoPE acts on each vector separately, so it still factors. The paper rotates the feature-mapped vectors:
\[
\text{Attn}(Q,K,V)_m = \frac{\sum_n \big(R^d_{\Theta,m}\phi(q_m)\big)^\top\big(R^d_{\Theta,n}\varphi(k_n)\big)\, v_n}{\sum_n \phi(q_m)^\top\varphi(k_n)}
\]
The denominator is left unrotated: rotated terms can be negative, and a sum of mixed-sign terms could hit zero. The numerator can then contain negative terms, so the weights are not strictly probabilities, but the paper argues they still model importance. The paper demonstrates this with a Performer (a linear-attention transformer) on enwik8, where adding RoPE lowered the training loss.

title: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE)
text:
8. Code
import numpy as np

def rope_freqs(d, base=10000.0):
    return base ** (-2.0 * np.arange(d // 2) / d)            # theta_i

def apply_rope(x, positions, base=10000.0):
    """x: (L, d), d even, interleaved pairs (x0,x1), (x2,x3), ...
    positions: (L,) integer positions."""
    L, d = x.shape
    ang = np.outer(positions, rope_freqs(d, base))           # (L, d/2): m * theta_i
    cos = np.repeat(np.cos(ang), 2, axis=1)                  # (L, d)
    sin = np.repeat(np.sin(ang), 2, axis=1)
    rot = np.empty_like(x)
    rot[:, 0::2], rot[:, 1::2] = -x[:, 1::2], x[:, 0::2]     # (-x2, x1, -x4, x3, ...)
    return x * cos + rot * sin

def rope_matrix(m, d, base=10000.0):                         # slow reference version
    R = np.zeros((d, d))
    for i, th in enumerate(rope_freqs(d, base)):
        c, s = np.cos(m * th), np.sin(m * th)
        R[2*i:2*i+2, 2*i:2*i+2] = [[c, -s], [s, c]]
    return R

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
d = 16
q, k = rng.normal(size=d), rng.normal(size=d)

# 1) the efficient form equals the matrix form
print(np.abs(apply_rope(q[None], [7])[0] - rope_matrix(7, d) @ q).max())   # ~0

# 2) the score depends only on the offset n - m
score = lambda m, n: apply_rope(q[None], [m])[0] @ apply_rope(k[None], [n])[0]
print(score(3, 10), score(103, 110), score(1003, 1010))                   # all equal
print(score(3, 10), score(3, 11))                                         # different offset

# 3) norms are preserved
print(np.linalg.norm(q), np.linalg.norm(apply_rope(q[None], [500])[0]))

# 4) caching rotated keys works: each key is rotated once, by its own position
K = rng.normal(size=(6, d)); Q = rng.normal(size=(6, d))
K_cached = apply_rope(K, np.arange(6))
full = apply_rope(Q, np.arange(6)) @ K_cached.T
step = apply_rope(Q[5:6], [5]) @ K_cached.T                                 # new token only
print(np.abs(full[5] - step[0]).max())                                      # ~0
KV cache. During generation, the keys of past tokens are cached. With plain RoPE you can cache keys after rotation: each key is rotated once by its own position, and a new query rotated by its own position gives the right relative score against all of them (check 4 above). One caveat appears in Part 3: methods that change the scaling as the sequence grows (dynamic scaling) require caching keys before rotation, because every token’s rotation changes when the scale changes.

title: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE)
text:
9. What the original evidence shows
It is worth knowing how modest the original experiments were, since RoPE’s current dominance comes mainly from later large-scale use:

WMT 2014 English-to-German translation: BLEU 27.5 for RoFormer versus 27.3 for the Transformer-base baseline.
BERT-style pre-training with RoPE in place of the position encoding: faster convergence of the masked-language-model loss.
GLUE fine-tuning: better on three of six tasks (MRPC, STS-B, QQP), worse on the other three (SST-2, QNLI, MNLI).
Chinese long documents (CAIL2019-SCM): accuracy improves when the input length goes from 512 to 1024 characters.

title: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE)
text:
Common pitfalls

Interleaved versus split-half pairing. Some code pairs dimensions \((2i, 2i+1)\) (as above); other code pairs \((i, i+d/2)\) and uses a “rotate half” trick. Both are valid if used consistently (they differ by a fixed permutation of dimensions), but pretrained weights assume one layout. Loading weights with the wrong convention silently wrecks the model.
Rotating \(V\) or the raw embeddings. Only \(q\) and \(k\), and after the projections.
Rotating \(q\) and \(k\) in different directions or with different bases. The relative-position identity needs the same rotation convention for both.
Odd head dimension. RoPE pairs dimensions, so \(d\) must be even.
Low-precision angles. At large positions \(m\theta_i\) is a large number and the cos and sin tables lose accuracy in float16 or bfloat16. A common practice is to compute the angles in float32.
“Relative” does not mean “extrapolates.” Plain RoPE still fails beyond the training length. The slow pairs never complete a full rotation within the training length, and the YaRN authors argue that this lets them act as absolute position markers; this is the observation that motivates Part 3.
Mixing up the sign convention (\(m-n\) versus \(n-m\)) when comparing formulas across papers. It only flips the direction of rotation.

title: From Token IDs to Vectors: How LLMs Embed Text
text:
A transformer cannot read text, and it can’t do much with integers either. Before any attention happens, every token ID must be converted into a vector of real numbers that capture its underlying meaning. This article covers that first step: what the embedding layer is, where its numbers come from, and why the shape of the resulting vector space matters for things like retrieval.
This is the follow-up to the tokenization article, which ended at the point where text has become a sequence of integer token IDs.

title: From Token IDs to Vectors: How LLMs Embed Text
text:
Why IDs are not enough
After tokenization, a sentence is a list of integers, for example [791, 4062, 14198]. Those integers are just labels. ID 4062 is not “more” of anything than ID 4061, so feeding them directly to a network would make it learn arithmetic on arbitrary labels.
The classic fix is one-hot encoding: for a vocabulary of size \(|V|\), token \(i\) becomes a vector of length \(|V|\) with a 1 at position \(i\) and 0 everywhere else. That removes the fake ordering, but it has two problems:

It is huge and almost entirely zeros (for \(|V| = 128{,}000\), one token is a 128,000-dimensional vector).
Every pair of distinct tokens is exactly equally far apart (there is no geometry). “king” is no closer to “queen” than to “bicycle”, so the encoding carries no notion of similarity.

An embedding replaces this with a short, dense, learned vector, typically a few thousand numbers, where similarity can be expressed by geometry.

title: From Token IDs to Vectors: How LLMs Embed Text
text:
The embedding table
The embedding layer is one matrix:
\[
\mathbf{E} \in \mathbb{R}^{|V| \times d}
\]

\(|V|\) is the vocabulary size (number of distinct tokens).
\(d\) is the embedding (model) dimension.
Row \(i\) of \(\mathbf{E}\) is the vector for token \(i\).

Embedding a token is just reading its row:
\[
\text{embed}(x_t) = \mathbf{E}[x_t] \in \mathbb{R}^{d}
\]
Here \(x_t\) is the token ID at position \(t\). For a sequence of \(n\) tokens \([x_1, \dots, x_n]\), stacking the rows gives the input to the first transformer layer:
\[
\mathbf{H}_0 = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{E}[x_1] \\ \vdots \\ \mathbf{E}[x_n] \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}
\]
Two things worth being clear about:

\(\mathbf{E}\) is a set of learned parameters, like any weight matrix. Unlike the tokenizer (which is fixed before training begins), the embedding table starts as random noise. The model stores one \(d\)-dimensional vector per token, and backpropagation adjusts those vectors alongside the rest of the network’s weights.
A lookup is mathematically a one-hot matrix product, which is why it is differentiable. If \(\mathbf{o}_i \in \{0, 1\}^{|V|}\) is the one-hot vector for token \(i\), then \(\mathbf{o}_i^\top \mathbf{E} = \mathbf{E}[i]\). In practice, frameworks skip the wasteful multiplication by zeros and index the row directly in \(O(1)\) time. Because it is equivalent to a linear projection, gradients flow cleanly during the backward pass, and only the rows for tokens present in the current batch receive updates, while the rest of the vocabulary receives a gradient of zero.






flowchart LR
    A["Text<br/>'The cat sat'"] --> B["Tokenizer"]
    B --> C["Token IDs<br/>[x1, x2, x3]"]
    C --> D["Embedding table, E<br/>(|V| x d)<br/>row lookups"]
    D --> E["Embeddings, H0<br/>(n x d)"]
    E --> F["Transformer<br/>layers"]







How big is it?
The table has \(|V| \times d\) numbers. For a configuration like Llama-3-8B (\(|V| = 128{,}256\), \(d = 4{,}096\)):
\[
128{,}256 \times 4{,}096 \approx 525\text{M parameters},
\]
roughly 6.5% of an ~8B-parameter model. The embedding table is a non-trivial slice of the model, and it grows linearly with the vocabulary, which is one reason vocabulary size is a design decision.

title: From Token IDs to Vectors: How LLMs Embed Text
section: Where do the vectors come from?
text:
Where do the vectors come from?
The table starts out random (for example normal or Xavier-style initialisation) and is trained by backpropagation together with the rest of the model. Nobody tells it that “king” and “queen” should be related. So why do related tokens end up close together?
The model is trained to predict the next token. Consider the contexts “The ___ barked at the mailman” and “I took my ___ for a walk”. Tokens that can fill the same slots (dog, puppy, hound) must make the downstream layers produce similar predictions, and the model eventually learns to give them similar vectors. This is the distributional hypothesis, usually quoted as “you shall know a word by the company it keeps” (Firth, 1957): similar contexts imply similar meaning, so the embedding table compresses that statistical structure into geometry.
Two training details:

Sparse updates on the input side. During a training step, only the rows of tokens that actually appeared in the batch receive gradient through the lookup. A token that is rarely seen gets few updates, so its row stays closer to its random starting point.
Weight tying. At the output, the model must turn a final hidden vector back into a score for every token in the vocabulary. That needs a \(d \times |V|\) matrix. Weight tying reuses the embedding matrix for this:

\[
\mathbf{W}_{\text{head}} = \mathbf{E}^\top
\]
So the logits (the raw scores before softmax) for a final hidden vector \(\mathbf{h}\) are \(\mathbf{h}\,\mathbf{E}^\top\): the model scores each token by how well \(\mathbf{h}\) lines up with that token’s embedding. Tying saves \(|V| \times d\) parameters and ties the “reading” and “writing” vocabularies together. Not every model does it (GPT-2 does; plenty of large models keep separate input and output matrices).
One consequence: with tying, every row of \(\mathbf{E}\) gets gradient updates from the output softmax as well, so the sparse-update picture above only describes the input lookup.

title: From Token IDs to Vectors: How LLMs Embed Text
text:
Measuring closeness: cosine similarity
To say two vectors are “close” we usually compare their directions with cosine similarity:
\[
\cos(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) = \frac{\mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{y}}{\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert\,\lVert\mathbf{y}\rVert}
\]
It is 1 when the vectors point the same way, 0 when they are orthogonal, and \(-1\) when opposite. Here \(\mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{y}\) is the dot product and \(\lVert\cdot\rVert\) the vector length.
Early static word vectors (word2vec-style) were shown to capture relationships as directions, the famous \(\vec{\text{king}} - \vec{\text{man}} + \vec{\text{woman}} \approx \vec{\text{queen}}\) (Mikolov et al., 2013). That is a property reported for those models and it is approximate; do not assume an LLM’s raw embedding table reliably does it.

title: From Token IDs to Vectors: How LLMs Embed Text
section: One vector per token is only the starting point
text:
One vector per token is only the starting point
The table gives each token one fixed vector, whatever the sentence. As the vectors pass through the layers they are mixed with context, so the vector for “bank” in “river bank” ends up different from “bank” in “bank loan”. These are the contextualized representations.
How much does context change them? Ethayarajh (2019) measured this for ELMo, BERT and GPT-2. After adjusting for a geometric effect (we discuss next), on average less than 5% of the variance in a word’s contextualized vectors can be explained by a single static vector for that word. So the layers do real work beyond the lookup table.

title: From Token IDs to Vectors: How LLMs Embed Text
text:
A geometry problem: anisotropy
There is a significant structural challenge in using these vectors for similarity search, clustering, or recommendation. If vectors were spread evenly over all directions (isotropic), two totally unrelated vectors would have cosine similarity about 0. Ethayarajh found that in practice, contextualized representations are anisotropic: they sit in a narrow cone, so random pairs already have a high cosine similarity. The anisotropy in GPT-2’s final layer is so extreme that any two random words have an almost perfect cosine similarity on average.





flowchart LR
    A["<b>Anisotropic</b><br/><small>• vectors in a narrow cone<br/>• random pair: cos ≈ 1</small>"] -- "whitening" --> B["<b>Isotropic</b><br/><small>• directions spread evenly<br/>• random pair: cos ≈ 0</small>"]






A common post-processing fix is whitening: shift the vectors so their mean is zero, then rotate and rescale so every direction has the same spread. In the notation of Su et al. (2021), with \(\mathbf{x}\) an embedding, \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) the mean embedding over a corpus, and \(\mathbf{W}\) a matrix computed from the corpus covariance:
\[
\tilde{\mathbf{x}} = (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})\,\mathbf{W}
\]
Keeping only the first \(k\) columns of \(\mathbf{W}\) also shrinks the vectors, which speeds up retrieval. In their experiments on sentence embeddings from BERT (whitening statistics fitted on the unlabeled evaluation sentences), this improved similarity scores on several benchmarks, for example STS-B Spearman correlation 59.04 → 71.34 for BERT-base, and a 768 → 256 dimension cut scored about the same (71.43). Gains are not uniform across datasets; the deep-dive article shows where it did not help.
To dive deeper, see the next article, Anisotropy and Whitening. It covers how isotropy is measured, what Ethayarajh’s experiments show, the derivation of \(\mathbf{W}\), the dimensionality-reduction trade-off, and a runnable demo.

title: From Token IDs to Vectors: How LLMs Embed Text
section: Code: lookup, one-hot equivalence, weight tying
text:
Code: lookup, one-hot equivalence, weight tying
This is a small PyTorch sketch (our own) showing the three ideas above.
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

V, d = 1000, 16                      # tiny vocabulary and dimension
emb = nn.Embedding(V, d)             # E: a learned (V x d) parameter matrix

ids = torch.tensor([3, 17, 3])       # a "sentence" of token IDs
H0 = emb(ids)                        # lookup -> shape (3, d)

# Lookup == one-hot @ E
one_hot = F.one_hot(ids, num_classes=V).float()   # (3, V)
assert torch.allclose(H0, one_hot @ emb.weight, atol=1e-6)

# Weight tying: the output head reuses E, so logits = h @ E^T
head = nn.Linear(d, V, bias=False)
head.weight = emb.weight             # same Parameter object: shared, not copied
h_final = torch.randn(3, d)          # stand-in for the final hidden states
logits = head(h_final)               # (3, V), equals h_final @ emb.weight.T

print(sum(p.numel() for p in {id(p): p for p in
          list(emb.parameters()) + list(head.parameters())}.values()))
# prints V*d = 16000, not 2*V*d, because the matrix is shared

cos = F.cosine_similarity(emb.weight[3], emb.weight[17], dim=0)
print(float(cos))                    # random-init rows: near 0 until trained

title: From Token IDs to Vectors: How LLMs Embed Text
text:
Common pitfalls

Treating the table as “meaning”. It is one context-free vector per token, and tokens are often sub-words, not words. Contextual meaning lives in the later layers.
Rare tokens. Rows for tokens seen rarely get only few updates during training, so their vectors can be poorly trained.
Weight tying and parameter counts. Tying shares one matrix between input and output; check whether a model ties before comparing parameter counts.
Trusting raw cosine similarity from a pretrained model. High baseline similarity between unrelated items is a known effect (as seen above). Check the baseline on your own data, and consider post-processing or an embedding model trained for similarity.
Fitting whitening on too little data. The covariance must be estimated from a representative corpus; see the deep dive.

title: The Cost of Attention: n², the KV Cache, GQA and MLA
text:
This is Part 7, the fourth and last article of this attention set. We know how attention works, how it is masked, and how multiple heads share the work. Now the bill: what does attention cost, and what do real systems do about it?
There are two different problems hiding under “attention is expensive”, and mixing them up is the most common source of confusion:

title: The Cost of Attention: n², the KV Cache, GQA and MLA
text:
Problem 1: the \(n^2\) score matrix
For a sequence of \(n\) tokens, the scores \(QK^\top\) form an \(n \times n\) matrix: every token against every token. Per layer, per head:

Time: \(O(n^2 \cdot d_k)\) multiply-adds to compute the scores (and the same order again to apply them to \(V\)).
Memory: \(O(n^2)\) to hold the score matrix if you store it.

Note that the size of the matrix depends only on \(n\), not on the model width. Here is how many entries it has, and how much memory that is for one head in one layer (binary units: 1 GiB = \(2^{30}\) bytes):

Doubling the context quadruples the cost. And these numbers are per head; a model has many heads (and the same again in every layer), though layers run one after another, so only one layer’s matrices need to exist at a time. A naive implementation that stores the full matrix simply cannot reach long contexts.

title: The Cost of Attention: n², the KV Cache, GQA and MLA
text:
Two phases of LLM inference
When an LLM answers a prompt, it works in two phases:

Prefill: the whole prompt is processed in one parallel pass (with the causal mask). This is where the \(n^2\) matrix appears.
Decode: tokens are then generated one at a time. Each new token needs attention over everything before it, but only one new query row, so there is no big square matrix. What dominates now is the cost of remembering the past. That is the KV cache.

title: The Cost of Attention: n², the KV Cache, GQA and MLA
text:
Problem 2: the KV cache
To generate token \(t+1\), the model computes a query for the new position and compares it with the keys of tokens \(1, \dots, t\), then takes a weighted sum of their values. The key and value vectors of earlier tokens do not change as generation proceeds, because with a causal mask a token’s representation never depends on later tokens. So we compute them once and store them. That stored collection is the KV cache.
Precisely, for every layer, every key/value head, and every token so far, the cache holds one key vector and one value vector (each of size \(d_\text{head}\)). What is not cached is the query: each query is used exactly once, for its own step, and then discarded.





flowchart LR
  T["<b>New token x_t</b>"] --> P["<b>Project</b><br/>q_t, k_t, v_t"]
  P -->|"append k_t, v_t"| C[("<b>KV cache</b><br/>k_1…k_t, v_1…v_t<br/>per layer, per KV head")]
  P -->|"q_t (used once)"| A["<b>Attention</b><br/>softmax(q_t·Kᵀ/√d_k)·V"]
  C -->|"all cached K, V"| A
  A --> N["<b>Next-token<br/>prediction</b>"]






Here is a minimal version for one head and one layer. The loop that reuses the cache produces exactly the same outputs as one full pass with a causal mask (we verified this numerically):
import numpy as np

def softmax(z, axis=-1):
    z = z - z.max(axis=axis, keepdims=True)
    e = np.exp(z)
    return e / e.sum(axis=axis, keepdims=True)

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n, d, d_k = 6, 16, 8
X = rng.standard_normal((n, d))
W_Q, W_K, W_V = (rng.standard_normal((d, d_k)) / np.sqrt(d) for _ in range(3))

# (a) one full pass with a causal mask
Q, K, V = X @ W_Q, X @ W_K, X @ W_V
M = np.triu(np.full((n, n), -np.inf), k=1)
full = softmax(Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(d_k) + M) @ V

# (b) token by token, with a KV cache
k_cache, v_cache, outs = [], [], []
for t in range(n):
    x_t = X[t]
    q_t = x_t @ W_Q                        # the query is used once and thrown away
    k_cache.append(x_t @ W_K)              # keys and values are appended and reused
    v_cache.append(x_t @ W_V)
    K_t, V_t = np.stack(k_cache), np.stack(v_cache)    # (t+1, d_k)
    w = softmax(q_t @ K_t.T / np.sqrt(d_k))            # (t+1,)
    outs.append(w @ V_t)

print(np.allclose(full, np.stack(outs)))   # True

How big is the cache?
Per token, the cache stores \(2\) (key and value) \(\times\) \(L\) layers \(\times\) \(n_\text{kv}\) KV heads \(\times\) \(d_\text{head}\) numbers:
\[
\text{cache bytes} = 2 \cdot L \cdot n_\text{kv} \cdot d_\text{head} \cdot \text{bytes per number} \cdot (\text{tokens}) \cdot (\text{batch size})
\]
Take a 7B to 8B-class configuration (as in Mistral 7B and Llama-3-8B): \(L = 32\) layers, 32 query heads, \(d_\text{head} = 128\), FP16 (2 bytes). With standard multi-head attention (32 KV heads) that is 512 KiB per token. With 8 KV heads, 128 KiB per token:

And that is for one sequence. Serving \(B\) requests at once multiplies it by \(B\). The cache grows linearly with context, but at long contexts and large batches it can rival the model weights in memory use. Since decoding is typically limited by how fast memory can be read, not by arithmetic, a smaller cache also means faster generation.

title: The Cost of Attention: n², the KV Cache, GQA and MLA
section: Shrinking the cache by sharing heads: MQA and GQA
text:
Shrinking the cache by sharing heads: MQA and GQA
The cache size is proportional to the number of KV heads. Standard multi-head attention gives every query head its own key and value head. Two ideas share them:

Multi-query attention (MQA) (Shazeer, 2019): all query heads share a single KV head.
Grouped-query attention (GQA) (Ainslie et al., 2023): an in-between setting. With \(h\) query heads and \(g\) KV heads (\(1 < g < h\)), each KV head is shared by a group of \(h/g\) query heads.

With 32 query heads and 8 KV heads, each KV head serves 4 query heads and the cache is 4 times smaller (the table above). The number of query heads is unchanged, so the score computation is the same; the savings are in cache memory and in the data read per decoding step.
In code, GQA is just sharing: compute fewer K and V heads, then repeat each across its group before attending:
h, g = 8, 2                                      # 8 query heads, 2 KV heads
Qh = ...                                         # (h, n, d_k)
Kg, Vg = ...                                     # (g, n, d_k): only g sets are computed and cached
Kh = np.repeat(Kg, h // g, axis=0)               # (h, n, d_k): heads 0-3 share KV head 0, heads 4-7 share KV head 1
Vh = np.repeat(Vg, h // g, axis=0)
out = softmax(Qh @ Kh.transpose(0, 2, 1) / np.sqrt(d_k) + M) @ Vh
The GQA paper reports that GQA reaches quality close to standard multi-head attention with speed comparable to MQA, and proposes converting an existing multi-head checkpoint by mean-pooling its key and value heads and then training briefly (about 5% of the original pre-training compute). Its experiments used T5 encoder-decoder models, so the exact numbers should not be assumed to transfer unchanged to every decoder-only LLM.

title: The Cost of Attention: n², the KV Cache, GQA and MLA
section: Shrinking the cache by compression: MLA
text:
Shrinking the cache by compression: MLA
GQA reduces the cache by having fewer KV heads. Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA), introduced with DeepSeek-V2 (DeepSeek-AI, 2024), keeps the full number of heads but compresses what is stored. For each token, the keys and values are jointly compressed into one small latent vector \(c_t\):
\[
c_t = W^{DKV} h_t, \qquad K_t = W^{UK} c_t, \qquad V_t = W^{UV} c_t
\]
Here \(h_t\) is the token’s hidden vector, \(W^{DKV}\) is a learned down-projection to a small size \(d_c\), and \(W^{UK}\), \(W^{UV}\) are learned up-projections that expand the latent back into per-head keys and values. Only \(c_t\) is cached, not \(K_t\) and \(V_t\).

What is actually cached. The paper adds a small extra “decoupled” key that carries positional information (rotary position embeddings, covered in the positional-encoding article), so the per-token cache is the latent plus that small key, not the latent alone.
Scale. DeepSeek-V2 uses 128 heads of size 128 and a latent size \(d_c = 512\). Standard attention would cache \(2 \times 128 \times 128 = 32{,}768\) numbers per token per layer for keys and values; the latent is 512 (plus the small positional key). The paper reports a 93.3% smaller KV cache and 5.76 times higher maximum generation throughput compared with their earlier DeepSeek 67B model; that comparison is between two different models, so it is not a pure measurement of MLA against standard attention.
Quality. The authors report that MLA matches or beats standard multi-head attention in their experiments, whereas MQA and GQA trade away some quality for their savings.
No free lunch. Reconstructing keys and values costs extra computation. The paper notes that at inference the up-projection matrices can be folded into the query and output projections, so full keys and values need not be explicitly built.




Variant

section: Taming the \(n^2\) cost: a map of the main ideas
text:
Taming the \(n^2\) cost: a map of the main ideas
These address problem 1 (and sometimes problem 2). Each deserves its own deep dive; the goal here is intuition.
1. FlashAttention: compute the same thing, move less data. FlashAttention (Dao et al., 2022) is an exact algorithm, not an approximation. GPUs have a large but slow main memory (HBM) and a tiny but very fast on-chip memory (SRAM). Standard attention writes the whole \(n \times n\) matrix to HBM and reads it back several times. FlashAttention processes the matrices in tiles that fit in SRAM, updating the softmax incrementally, so the full matrix is never written to HBM. The paper reports memory that is linear in sequence length and large wall-clock speedups. The number of arithmetic operations is not reduced (the backward pass even recomputes some values); the win is fewer memory reads and writes, which is what limits attention in practice.
2. Sliding-window (local) attention: look only nearby. Each token attends to only the previous \(w\) tokens, so cost is \(O(n \cdot w)\), linear in \(n\). Longformer (Beltagy et al., 2020) and Mistral 7B (Jiang et al., 2023, window 4,096) use this. Information can still travel further, because each layer lets a token see \(w\) positions back from tokens that themselves already saw \(w\) positions back; in principle after \(L\) layers the reach is about \(L \cdot w\), but that indirect path is weaker than direct attention.
3. Sparse patterns: local plus a few long-range links. Combine a local window with a few global tokens that attend to (and are attended by) everything. BigBird (Zaheer et al., 2020) adds random links and reports cost linear in sequence length. The earlier Sparse Transformer (Child et al., 2019) reduced the cost to \(O(n\sqrt{n})\).
4. Linear attention and state-space models: change the math. Without the softmax, \((\phi(Q)\phi(K)^\top)V\) can be regrouped by associativity as \(\phi(Q)\,(\phi(K)^\top V)\). The small matrix \(\phi(K)^\top V\) is computed once, giving cost linear in \(n\). Models such as Mamba (Gu & Dao, 2023) and RWKV (Peng et al., 2023) follow this recurrent-style direction. These are different architectures rather than drop-in replacements, and results vary on tasks that need precise recall of specific earlier tokens, so they are usually evaluated carefully against full attention.
5. KV-cache compression and eviction: remember less. Keep the cache bounded by dropping or shrinking entries. H2O (Zhang et al., 2023) keeps the tokens that have received the most attention plus recent ones. StreamingLLM (Xiao et al., 2023) keeps the first few “attention sink” tokens plus a recent window. Quantized caches store keys and values in lower precision.

A useful way to keep these straight: masks and sparsity decide which scores exist; FlashAttention decides how the existing scores are computed; GQA, MLA and eviction decide what is remembered between steps. FlashAttention composes with masks such as sliding windows rather than competing with them.

title: The Cost of Attention: n², the KV Cache, GQA and MLA
text:
Common pitfalls

Saying FlashAttention “reduces the complexity”. It is exact attention with the same \(O(n^2)\) arithmetic; it reduces memory traffic and avoids storing the \(n \times n\) matrix.
Quoting the score-matrix size without “per head, per layer”, or tying it to the model width. It depends only on \(n\) (and the number of bytes per entry).
Confusing the two problems. The \(n^2\) matrix is transient and mainly a prefill problem. The KV cache is persistent and grows with every generated token and every concurrent request.
Caching queries, or thinking the cache stores text. The cache holds keys and values (per layer, per KV head), not queries and not tokens.
Forgetting layers and batch size in cache estimates. Memory scales with \(L \times n_\text{kv} \times d_\text{head} \times \text{tokens} \times \text{batch}\).
Reading GQA as “fewer attention heads”. The number of query heads stays the same; only the number of distinct key/value heads shrinks.
Treating MLA as GQA with a different name. MLA keeps all heads and stores a compressed latent from which keys and values are rebuilt.
Mixing units. GB (powers of 10) and GiB (powers of 2) differ by about 7%, which matters at the 64 GiB scale.

title: The Cost of Attention: n², the KV Cache, GQA and MLA
text:
Summary

Attention’s score matrix is \(n \times n\) per head per layer, so time and naive memory grow quadratically with context.
The KV cache stores each layer’s keys and values for all past tokens, so decoding does not recompute them. Its size grows linearly with context, layers, KV heads and batch.
GQA shrinks the cache by sharing KV heads across groups of query heads; MLA shrinks it by caching a low-rank latent per token.
FlashAttention makes exact attention fast and memory-light; sliding windows, sparse patterns, linear attention and cache eviction trade some generality for lower cost.
